📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Cricut Maker 5 isn't a significant leap from the Maker 4, but it's smaller, lighter, easier to set up and can cut materials up to 3mm thick. It also keeps the versatility that makes the Maker range so appealing, from intricate paper designs and vinyl stickers to engraving metal and cutting fabric.

Smaller and lighter than earlier Makers.

Huge range of tools and materials.

Up to twice as fast as the Maker 3.

Little reason for Maker 4 owners to upgrade.

Rotary blade, knife blade and FabricGrip mat cost extra.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Price: $349 / £349.99 machine only, $399 / £399.99 Essential Bundle, $529 / £499.99 Ultimate Bundle.

Dimensions: 50.2 x 19.1 x 11.9cm.

Cutting speed: Up to 14.1 inches per second.

Materials support: 300+ compatible materials.

Maximum cutting speed: 3mm (depending on material and tool).

Compatible tools: 13, including engraving.

Maximum Smart Material cut length: 3.6m (12ft).

Maximum cut area: 29.2 x 59.7cm with a large mat.

Connectivity: Bluetooth Low Energy, USB-C.

In a recent development, I've been using Cricut machines for years, mostly for quilting and personalised craft projects, and what keeps me coming back to the Maker range is how much one machine can do. The Maker 5 keeps that going. Cuts are accurate, it's quick, and Design Space makes projects easy to start, whether you work from a template or design your own.

If you own the older Maker 3, I'd seriously consider upgrading: the faster cutting and more compact body are noticeable straight away. If you already have the slightly newer Maker 4, it's a harder argument to make, because Maker 5 tidies up the older machine and makes subtle improvements rather than replacing it, and the Maker 4 is still an excellent cutter.

Recent findings suggest that for anyone choosing a first Cricut, the Maker 5 is a great option, provided you'll use its extra capabilities. If you mostly make cards, stickers and vinyl decorations, the cheaper Explore range may be all you need.

In this Maker 5 review, I go into detail on what the fresh craft machine can do, how to use it, and how it compares with recent Cricut releases.

The first thing I noticed was the colour. The Slate Blue finish is a soft grey-blue that looks more contemporary than earlier Makers. It's also a lot smaller, with Cricut claiming a 30% reduction in size compared with earlier machines. At around 50cm wide, 19cm deep and 12cm high, it takes up noticeably less room on my desk, and at 4.9kg it's lighter than the Maker 4, so it's easy to move or put away. That's handy if you have a dedicated craft room, and even more so if, like me, you sometimes have to share your workspace with other projects.

The lid includes a storage tray to keep tools close at hand, and the overall design feels neat and considered.

In a recent development, setup is straightforward. Head to the Cricut website, select the Maker 5 and follow the instructions. It tells you how much room you need in front of and behind the machine for materials and mats to feed through, and reminds you to remove the packaging before you start. Plug it in, open Design Space on your computer, and follow the prompts. The machine connects over Bluetooth; there's no separate on/off switch to worry about, and the software talks you through loading material and starting each job.

Recent findings suggest that the Maker 5 comes with a 12 x 12 in LightGrip mat, a cutting tool, a scoring tool, and a dual-sided black marker, plus materials for your first project. Depending on the bundle, you may also get a portable trimmer.

According to recent reports, if you're upgrading from an older Cricut, many of your existing tools carry over, including mats, fine-point blades, and many older Maker tools, as well as Smart Materials such as vinyl and iron-on. The upcoming snap-in pen holder has different compatibility requirements, though, so check your pens before assuming they'll fit.

According to recent reports, the rotary blade for cutting fabric and specialist blades such as the knife blade for thicker materials are extra purchases. They matter most if you're buying the Maker for quilting or more ambitious projects.

The Maker 5 cuts up to 14.1 inches per second, which is fast, but the Maker 4 already offered that speed, so don't expect a dramatic difference if you're upgrading from that model. Maker 3 owners will notice more: like the Maker 4, the Maker 5 cuts up to twice as fast, which really highlights when you're working through multiple designs or larger projects.

Sources indicate that it handles more than 300 compatible materials, from delicate paper and vinyl to leather, fabric and selected thicker materials. It can cut, draw, score, engrave and deboss, and it works with a home printer for full-colour Print Then Cut projects.

Industry observers note that smart Materials are a significant part of the Cricut experience. They feed straight into the machine without a cutting mat, which makes longer designs much easier. Smart Vinyl, for example, can be loaded directly for continuous cuts of up to 12ft. Leftover vinyl doesn't have to go to waste either, as you can stick smaller pieces onto a Cricut mat.

According to recent reports, for standard cardstock, vinyl and iron-on projects, the Maker 5 is very easy to use. Design Space tells you which material to select, which blade or tool to load and when to feed the mat into the machine, so you spend more time creating and less time worrying about settings.

In a recent development, this is where the Maker 5 earns its place as Cricut's flagship. The Explore range handles everyday crafting well, but I'd recommend the Maker to anyone serious about quilting, sewing or fabric projects. In fact, anything that requires more power and precision.

It has been revealed that the rotary blade cuts fabric accurately and quickly, without endless measuring or hand-cutting shapes. You'll need to buy the rotary blade and housing separately, along with a pink FabricGrip mat, available in 12 x 12 inches and 12 x 24 inches.

For quilters, that's a huge time-saver. Design Space offers a selection of quilting blocks and templates, with components separated into shapes and colours, ready for cutting. Take the half-square triangle, a quilting staple that's surprisingly fiddly to cut by hand. You're cutting on the bias, so accuracy matters if the pieces are going to line up.

Sources indicate that in Design Space, I create a square, add a diagonal line and change the line operation to Cut. After rotating it by 45 degrees, I position it over the square, select both elements and attach them. The result is two accurately cut triangles, ready to use. When you're making a quilt with dozens or even hundreds of identical pieces, having the machine do the repetitive cutting makes a real difference.

According to recent reports, the Maker can also handle thicker, more demanding materials than the Explore machines, up to 3mm. Add a knife blade, another extra, and selected wood and chipboard projects open up too.

According to recent reports, engraving is one of my favourite things about the Maker 5. I photographed my house, uploaded it to Design Space, and used the software to prepare the image for engraving on an aluminium sheet. I was thrilled with the result. The machine picked out the lines and architectural details of the building, making a personalised piece that would suit a keepsake or gift. It's the kind of project that indicates why I'd pick a Maker over an Explore if you want to experiment with different materials and techniques.

According to recent reports, I also used the Maker 5 to engrave and colour a set of toothbrush gifts (pictured) for someone in my village. The process was challenging but fun, and the Maker 5 powered through the set with ease.

The engraving tool works with the Maker 5, but it isn't included in every bundle, so check what you're buying. You can also buy it separately, and Cricut sells suitable metal and acrylic blanks. With the right tools, the machine can also deboss, score, and perforate, leaving plenty of room to experiment beyond straightforward cutting.

Personalised vinyl lettering is one of the easiest projects to start with. I've used Design Space to make name tags for items that need a little personalisation. Select Text from the menu, type the names, and choose your font and size. When you're happy with the design, load your Smart Permanent Vinyl with the coloured side facing up. The machine cuts around the letters, leaving you to remove the unwanted vinyl.

This is where patience and a micro-weeding tool come in handy. The tiny pieces inside letters such as 'e' and 'a' can be fiddly to pick out, particularly in smaller text. Next, cut a piece of transfer tape, peel off the backing, and place it over the design. Use a scraper to make sure the lettering sticks to the tape, then lift it away and press it onto your chosen surface. Permanent vinyl is already adhesive-backed, so you don't need any extra glue.

It has been revealed that iron-on vinyl works similarly, with two key differences. Switch on Mirror in Design Space before cutting, and place the iron-on with its shiny side down on the mat. That way, the lettering reads correctly when you transfer it to fabric with a heat press.

In a recent development, print Then Cut is one of the most useful features if you like making colourful stickers, gift labels or personalised stationery. Instead of being limited to vinyl colours and effects, you print a full-colour design on your home printer and let the Cricut cut around the individual shapes.

Sources indicate that I use it for Christmas present labels. Create your design in Design Space, select Print Then Cut and send it to your printer. Once it's printed onto suitable printable vinyl or sticker paper, place the sheet on the Cricut mat and load it into the machine. The Maker 5 reads the registration marks and cuts around the printed designs, giving you colourful stickers with neat edges.

You'll need to buy printable vinyl or sticker paper separately, though, and the final results depend on your printer as well as the Cricut.

If you enjoy paper crafting, Design Space offers plenty to explore. You can choose pre-made templates, edit existing projects or start from scratch with your own images, shapes and text.

According to recent reports, I've used it to make personalised Christmas gift tags, combining the machine's drawing and cutting functions. For one design, I set the machine to write a name with the pen, then switched to the fine-point blade to cut out the tag. For another, I used the blade to cut the lettering itself, which gives a different finish. Being able to write and cut in one project is useful, and Design Space makes it easy to arrange everything before you send the job to the machine.

You can also make paper flowers, boxes, cards, and Christmas decorations, with a huge range of templates you can customise in different colours, fonts, and materials. The included scoring tool helps here, giving you clean fold lines for cards and boxes.

Industry observers note that foil is another way to give cards, gift tags and decorations a more professional finish. The Maker 5 supports Cricut's Foil Transfer Tool, but you'll need to buy the tool and foil sheets separately.

I used the Cricut Foil Transfer Kit, which costs around £43.49 and includes the tool, foil sheets and adhesive strips. It took me three attempts to get the result I wanted, but once I'd got the hang of it, the finish was excellent.

A few tips if you're trying it yourself:.

Sources indicate that once it's finished, unload the mat and carefully remove your card. The metallic detail makes handmade cards and gifts look far more polished.

You control the Maker 5 through Cricut Design Space, which is available on desktop and mobile. It's easy to install and walks you through each stage of a project. There's a huge library of ready-made designs, templates, and fonts, so you don't need to be confident with graphic design to get started; you can upload your own images or build designs from scratch.

Cricut has also added AI-assisted image generation, which is handy if you have an idea but don't have the illustration skills or software to create the artwork yourself.

Industry observers note that the basic Design Space app is free, and you don't need a Cricut Access subscription to operate the machine. Access unlocks a much larger library of images, fonts, and ready-made projects, and some features and content depend on it, so it's worth factoring the ongoing cost into your budget if you expect to use the library regularly.

What I like most is how the software guides you through the making process. Pick your project, choose your material, follow the instructions, and the machine does the hard work while you focus on the creative side.

Choosing a Cricut can be confusing with so many models around. The Maker 5 sits at the top of the range, but that doesn't mean it's right for everyone.

The Maker 4 is still very capable, and the two share much of the same cutting performance and tool compatibility.

The Maker 5 is smaller and lighter, has USB-C connectivity and a revised tool and pen-loading system, and handles compatible materials up to 3mm thick, compared with the Maker 4's 2.4mm.

Recent findings suggest that both cut at up to 14.1 inches per second, so there's no speed advantage. If you already own a Maker 4, I'd only switch if the smaller footprint, lighter body or workflow improvements matter to you.

In a recent development, the Explore 5 is much more affordable and ideal for everyday crafting. It handles vinyl, paper, cardstock and iron-on materials, and it's a great choice for stickers, cards, personalised gifts and decorations. It doesn't have the Maker's full range of tools, though.

If you're a quilter, want to cut fabric with a rotary blade, engrave metal, or work with more demanding materials, choose the Maker 5.

Industry observers note that for many hobby crafters, the Explore 5 will be perfectly adequate. But if you want to grow into more ambitious projects, the Maker gives you far more flexibility.

Sources indicate that the Cricut Maker 5 is an excellent cutting machine, and versatility remains its biggest strength. Whether you're making personalised labels, Christmas decorations, paper flowers, cards, fabric patterns, or engraved keepsakes, it can do very little with the right tool and material.

I like how easy it is to set up and use. The smaller size is welcome; the lighter body makes it easier to move around, and the software takes much of the guesswork out of creating projects. Print Then Cut is great, and the engraving highlights how much potential there is beyond everyday vinyl and paper crafts.

The extras add up, though. For quilting, you'll need a rotary blade and FabricGrip mat. Engraving, foiling and other specialist projects need their own tools and materials, and printable vinyl is another cost if you initiative to make stickers. The supplied cardstock is useful for getting started, but I found it stuck to the mat when I tried to remove it, so peel it away carefully.

It has been revealed that if you're upgrading from a Maker 3, the doubled cutting speed makes a compelling case. Maker 4 owners should be more cautious, as the smaller design and extra material thickness are useful, but the cutting performance is largely the same.

Recent findings suggest that for anyone buying their first serious Cricut, though, the Maker 5 is a smart buy. It's easy to use, surprisingly compact for what it can do, and it lets you experiment with a huge range of projects. If you're a quilter or someone who likes to make a little bit of everything, this is the Cricut I'd choose.

Julie Dean is a former doctor and occupational therapist by profession, which inspired her to start sewing and quilting as a therapeutic activity. She is passionate about her craft and has been quilting and using Cricut for over five years. As well as selling her own designs and products on Etsy, Julie has taken commissions for interior design agencies to create bespoke quilts, including Beata Heuman. Julie's work has appeared in Architectural Digest.

Mutabor Unveils the Voith brand identity

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.
  • The whole system starts with a single chevron.
  • Sources indicate that the custom typeface carries the voice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.

The whole system starts with a single chevron. Mutabor calls it the V-Vector, a > that points forward and never sits still: it repeats into a pattern on the Appleton reception wall, frames a machine on the launch poster, and turns into punctuation inside the headlines. Voith Blue stays the signature color, and bright tones join it, a vivid royal blue for screens and a mint green for the accent word. On black, "Machines with a digital heart." puts the machine inside the chevron. On blue, "Always breaking latest ground" lets the green >ground do the talking.

Sources indicate that the custom typeface carries the voice. Mutabor drew it only for Voith, and it highlights in the way headlines sit: heavy, round, and set large enough that one line fills a poster. "Hydro driving renewable momentum" runs white on blue with the green >momentum as the punchline, and "Speed press" splits across a dark panel in the same weight. The VOITH wordmark stays in solid capitals, unchanged, while the type around it changes scale.

According to recent reports, one frame shows the construction behind it, a lowercase a drawn with node points and thin rules beside a turbine, the letter treated like an engineered part. The grid is visible in the letterform, and the same precision runs through the system, from the wordmark lockup to the small labels on the machine diagrams.

The system proves itself where the manufacturer actually works. The reception wall at Appleton carries the blue V pattern behind "Welcome to Appleton", with the VOITH wordmark set into the desk. Posters, phone screens, documents, and an agenda share the same blue, the same green, and the same chevron, from a "We are hiring" phone card to a "CSH operating principle" diagram. A purple machine close-up is labeled "nanometer precision torque drive", the product photography sitting inside the same graphic language as the posters.

Some of the case imagery is marked AI generated, Mutabor's own label on the frames, and the photography of the plants and machines reads as illustration as much as record. The rollout began in March 2026, after an internal launch in October 2025, and now runs across all markets and touchpoints. It is the first time the three business units, hydropower, papermaking, and drive technology, share one consistent, digitally native identity, and the work took the Red Dot Award for Corporate Design and Identity in 2026.

Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year winner named

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2489 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.
  • The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.
  • Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.

The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.

V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility.

The master jury cited the project as a “sophisticated wayfinding scheme that demonstrates how signage can do far more than direct: it can define identity, shape experience and establish a sense of place”.

The judges praised the design for its “clarity, confidence and restraint, seamlessly guiding visitors through the V&A East Storehouse while adding to the character of the building”.

V&A East Storehouse was up against designs that included a constellation of gloopy-looking polished resin lights, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van and a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

Read more about all the winning design projects below:.

Design project of the year and graphic design of the year: V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility.

Design studio Fieldwork Facility was challenged with navigating visitors to the V&A’s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse.

The Hackney design studio looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse: Gen-Z apps and services.

“This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse,” noted the master jury.

“As the displays change, the signage, captions and general wayfinding can be updated efficiently, embracing the adaptability and lack of formality of the museum.”.

Furniture design of the year: Dado Series by Allen Kaufmann Objects.

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten won furniture design of the year for its Dado series of tables and shelves.

What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial.

The practice adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools nor glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners.

“What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial,” the judges stated. “The shelving is satisfying to assemble and demonstrates everything furniture needs to be, and no more.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Seating design of the year: Kino by Pablo Castillo Design.

Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo won seating design of the year for Kino, a cantilevered 3D-printed chair for Decibel.

Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

Recent findings suggest that its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

“The 3D printing of furniture is becoming more refined and this is a strong example of that,” stated the master jury.

It has been revealed that “The mono-material construction is sophisticated and has a strong aesthetic profile,” they continued. “Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.”.

Collectible design of the year: Lima Charlie by Studio Laurids Gallée.

Austrian designer Laurids Gallée won collectible design of the year for Lima Charlie, a series of five colourful, sculptural lamps.

Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship.

The lighting collection comprises five hand-cast resin light works and machined aluminium pieces.

It has been revealed that first, the designer used digital processes to determine each composition. Then, casting solid blocks of the material before colouring, cutting and sculpting them into shape. Each piece was meticulously sanded and polished to arrive at the desired smooth surface.

“Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship,” praised the judges. “Beautiful treasures to enhance any space.”.

Bespoke design of the year: Real Time Schiphol People’s Clock by Maarten Baas.

Dutch designer Maarten Baas won bespoke design of the year for The People’s Clock, a choreographed representation of the passage of time at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.

It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.

Baas recruited 1,000 participants – the majority being airport employees – to form the hands of The People’s Clock and move in sync, forming the hour and minute hands. The second hand comprises a single person running a lap of the circular perimeter each minute.

“This timepiece in Amsterdam’s busy airport momentarily takes users away from the efficient functionality of the space by providing a reference to the time in a more playful and poetic way,” mentioned the master jury.

“It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.”.

Lighting design of the year: Hoop Table Lamp by John Tree for Vaarnii.

Designer John Tree won lighting design of the year for the Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni.

There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.

The monolithic light combines a block of solid pine wood – synonymous with the Finnish brand’s designs – with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer, sourced from a sustainably managed forest.

“We were all drawn to the simple and characterful gestures of this table lamp, which embraces warmth from a common timber,” the judges said.

“There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.”.

Architectural lighting design of the year: Cologne Cathedral by Licht Kunst Licht.

Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht won architectural lighting design of the year for its illumination of Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade.

This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline.

The lighting scheme used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

“This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline,” the judges praised.

“The light sources are subtly integrated and have managed to reduce energy consumption while creating maximum impact for this city landmark,” they added.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Surface design of the year: Basic Third by Pretty Plastic.

Dutch manufacturer Pretty Plastic won surface design of the year for its Basic Third tiles.

There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.

The cladding material was developed by the Pretty Plastic company, started by architecture studios Overtreders W and Bureau SLA.

The tiles, which were made from 30,987 kilograms of post-consumer plastic waste, have been applied as cladding for Plus Ultra III, the first timber laboratory building in the Netherlands.

“Pretty Plastics has chosen to work with the worst kind of plastic – PVC – and found a way to repurpose the material into tiles,” remarked the judges.

In a recent development, “The material is already fire-compliant and UV stable, making it a worthy contender for the cladding of buildings,” they continued. “There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.”.

Looking ahead, the judges mentioned “its impact will be proven by how easy it is to scale.”.

Textile design of the year: Bianni Wool Paper by Arudeko.

Mexican design studio won textile design of the year for Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool.

With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

Bianni can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

“With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste,” the judges commended.

Sources indicate that “Furthermore, the processing provides employment to skilled locals, the outcome being an interesting and beautiful paper alternative to be applied to other products,” they stated. “There is much potential for further exploration across the world.”.

Workplace design of the year: Area by Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Foster + Partners and Kettal won workplace design of the year for their modular Area table system.

There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition.

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power. The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

“There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition,” noted the judges.

“There are sophisticated elements and thoughtful hidden details for integrating technology into an otherwise minimalist design,” they continued.

Product design (consumer design) of the year: Pedal 4 by Minimal.

British start-up Minimal won product design (consumer design) of the year for Pedal 4, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van.

A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries.

The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets. It is now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

“A smart upcoming vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries,” praised the judges.

Sources indicate that “This is a great ‘last mile’ replacement for large polluting vans. The slender design manoeuvres easily in city streets while the electric motor emits no noxious pollutants,” they continued.

“The vehicles’ local assembly also allows it to be easily repaired.”.

Product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year: CurifyLabs PharmaPrinter Aurum by Studio Aslak Siimes.

Industrial design firm Studio Aslak Siimes and Finnish startup CurifyLabs won product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year for pharmaceutical compounding system, PharmaPrinter Aurum.

It’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered.

The system is designed to improve the process of creating patient-specific medicine, born from the realisation that almost 30 per cent of all medication requires personalisation rather than being mass-manufactured, according to studio founder Aslak Siimes.

According to recent reports, “This device offers a real innovation in precision healthcare and decentralises the production of pills,” the judges said. “Precise medical doses are prepared bespoke for each customer, reducing waste and eliminating human error.”.

“Furthermore, it’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered,” they added.

Product design (bathroom) of the year: Dekoda by Kohler Health.

Kohler Health won product design (bathroom) of the year for Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet.

This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions.

Designed to be discreet and intuitive, the tracker clips to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

It has been revealed that “This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions,” the judges said. “The design of the device is discreet and visually passive, making it suitable for its function in the bathroom.”.

Installation design of the year: Einder for USB002 Tour by Boris Acket and Fred Again.

Visual artist Boris Acket won installation design of the year for Einder, which featured as the standout show design for DJ Fred again..’s USB002 Tour.

It has been revealed that this lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!

The installation features a large suspended sheet of fabric which floats above the audience like a transparent, breathing roof.

Throughout the concert, the sculpture wafts and moves across the audience, creating smaller and larger spaces, static spatial gestures, storms, and water surfaces.

The judges summed up the project as “stunning, emotive, immersive, dynamic, simple”.

“This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!”.

Sustainable design of the year: Datecrete by Datecrete Studio.

Architect Sara Abu Farha and engineer Khaled Shalka won sustainable design of the year for Datecrete, a concrete-style material developed by Abu Farha and Shalka formed from crushed dates.

This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete.

According to recent reports, the project aims to demonstrate how the abundant regional byproduct can become part of an architectural material language. Patent-pending, Datecrete can be produced as floor and wall tiles, cladding, furniture, lighting elements and smaller design objects.

“This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete,” mentioned the master jury.

“The processing of the pits is decentralised, so it has the potential to scale in communities across the date-growing region.”.

Material innovation of the year: Mimmik Tile by Front.

Dutch sustainability platform Front and biotechnology company Biomason won material innovation of the year for Mimmik, a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete.

Front believes Mimmik is the first bacteria-grown tile to be industrially produced, making a sustainable technology available to a wide market of specifiers looking to reduce the carbon footprint of their commercial projects.

“This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete,” praised the judges.

“As such, the embodied carbon is greatly reduced,” they noted. “The production is scalable and could shift the dial in the future production of tiles and paving.”.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

Industry News: Van Gogh’s record-breaking ‘Blossoming Chestnut Trees’: the $190m sale and the restitution claim that nearly upended it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's Upcoming York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees.
  • Recent findings suggest that the auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in.
  • Before the auction, Sotheby’s had not revealed a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's Upcoming York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees. Auctioneer Oliver Barker began the sale by stating that “the work is being offered for sale pursuant to an agreement between the seller and the heirs of the Hedwig and Samuel Fischer family”. The Fischer family had sold the painting in 1936.

Recent findings suggest that the auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in. A third bidder, in the saleroom, won the contest after less than four minutes, at a hammer price of $165m. He is the Newly introduced York dealer William Acquavella, presumably acting for an unidentified client.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (May 1890).

Before the auction, Sotheby’s had not revealed a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees). This may have been slightly optimistic, since it was far more than any Van Gogh has ever made. Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) is a fine landscape, although not among his very best. And the other 11 pictures in last night’s auction of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection generally sold for around, or even below, their lower estimates.

According to recent reports, the uncertainty last weekend over a possible Nazi-era claim for the Van Gogh may have discouraged some potential bidders, but the $190m (including fees) was nonetheless an astonishing result. This was for an artist who had failed to sell during his own lifetime. Van Gogh completed nearly a thousand paintings in his career, with only a single recorded sale: The Red Vineyard (November 1888, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow).

Only three artworks have ever sold for more at auction: Leonardo’s Salvator Mundi (around 1500, $450m, Christie’s, 2017), Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1916, $236m, Sotheby’s, 2025) and Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn (1964, $195m, Christie’s, 2022).

The previous record price for a Van Gogh was $117m (including fees) for Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888), which Christie’s sold in 2022. The Blossoming Chestnut Trees price was 62% more.

Sotheby’s has been open about Blossoming Chestnut Trees’s Nazi-era (1933-45) provenance. Following our inquiries, we reported in our 2 October blog post: “It was purchased four years later [in 1926] by the Berlin-based publisher Samuel Fischer, and on his death in 1934 it passed to his daughter Brigitte. Although the family was persecuted because of their Jewish heritage, a Sotheby’s spokesperson confirmed to us that, based on recent research, the family was free at all times to dispose of the painting.”.

Literaturport.de via Wikimedia Commons.

News of a possible Nazi-era claim emerged only five weeks later. Berlin-based Gunnar Schnabel, who describes himself as a “looted art researcher” specialising in the Nazi period, told the New York Times that he first heard about the sale on 7 November, when he was “lying on a sofa in his vacation home”. His letter to Sotheby’s calling for the sale to be delayed was sent on 12 November, just six days before the auction. Obviously this put Sotheby’s in a very awkward situation: should the sale be postponed or go ahead?

In response, Sotheby’s stated: “We are aware of the persecution experienced by the Fischer family. After the Anschluss in 1938, the family fled Austria, and the Gestapo confiscated their Vienna home, library and remaining art collection. But the circumstances around this transaction were different”. The auction house also added that after the war, no claim was ever made for the Van Gogh.

Recent findings suggest that urgent negotiations were held with the representatives of the Fischer family. The key question at stake was whether their ancestors had been the victim of a forced sale at a lower than market value. By June 1936, when the Van Gogh was sold, the family had just moved to Vienna. They had consigned the painting to the Cassirer gallery in Amsterdam several years earlier, in 1932-33. The price eventually paid in 1936 by the buyer, Paris-based collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer, was $22,000.

Industry observers note that comparisons with other Van Gogh sales around the time are telling. In 1935, the year before the Fischer sale, Orchard with Cypresses had sold for $15,000 at the Latest York auction house Parke Bernet (this was the painting which later fetched a record Van Gogh price in 2022). That makes the $22,000 seem reasonable.

Then there is the Sunflowers (August 1888), which had been sold to London's National Gallery in 1924 for the equivalent of $5,800. Although this sale took place 12 years before Blossoming Chestnut Trees and Jo Bonger, Vincent’s sister-in-law, probably reduced the price for a major museum, it is now regarded as Van Gogh’s greatest masterpiece. This again suggests that the Fischers received a reasonable sum for their picture.

Sources indicate that following yesterday’s Sotheby’s auction, Schnabel told The Art Newspaper that the Fischers had also been supported by the Commission for Looted Art in Europe's co-chair Anne Webber. He added that the family is delighted that Blossoming Chestnut Trees “which hung in the Berlin home of Samuel and Hedwig Fischer for a quarter of a century, has now found a new owner”. They hope this case “may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era, and that they, too, may find a path toward the recognition of their rightful claims.”.

The terms of the 17 November settlement between the heirs of the Fischer family and the Blaquier-Arrieta family remain confidential. Presumably some sort of financial compensation has been paid. The agreement opens the door for the Fischer heirs to make claims for further paintings which had once been in their family if they come onto the market in the future.

Title page of the Leicester Galleries exhibition Artists who Died Young, with an image of Blossoming Chestnut Trees.

As a postscript on the 1930s story of Blossoming Chestnut Trees, soon after the Kapferers bought the picture they lent it to an exhibition in London, Artists who Died Young at the Leicester Galleries in 1938. A year after the London exhibition, war broke out. Blossoming Chestnut Trees had been sent to the United States a few months earlier to Fresh York dealers Wildenstein & Co and, after passing through two American private collections, it went to Argentina in 1975, to the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Following the Sotheby’s sale, it remains a mystery where the Van Gogh will ultimately reside.

Sources indicate that martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin Bailey’s recent Van Gogh books.

It has been revealed that martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I've been talking a lot lately about how Apple seems to have rediscovered its sense of fun. From folding iPhones to touchscreen MacBooks, via an uncharacteristically zany latest TikTok presence, the tech giant is doing a lot to persuade us it's in a more playful mode of late. But if Apple really wants to convince me it's here for a good time, it needs to make these nostalgic AirPods a reality.

The iMac G3 days have become synonymous with the halcyon days of Y2K tech design. Think bold citrus colours and translucent plastic. Those colours have made an unexpected return with the latest iMac and, of course, the MacBook Neo. Apple's in-ear AirPods, however, remain available in any colour you like – as long as it's white. But wouldn't a splash of Y2K colour make them so much more fun?

A post shared by Krishnavi Anand Krishnavi (@blessed_krishnavi).

Concept artist Krishnavi Anand Krishnavi has been sharing nostalgic Apple product concepts on Instagram for a while, including an iPhone SE revival I would love to see. But it's the 'AirPods G3' that are the most fun, with their noughties design sensibilities. There's a lot going on inside an AirPod, and that colourful translucent plastic tantalisingly reveals some of its secrets.

"Apple might get me if they bring back these gems," one Instagram user comments, while another adds, "If these don’t actually come out I will sue." Another rather dispiritingly chimes in, "Apple will never do something this fun and imaginative.".

But we are seeing more imagination from Apple lately, at least when it comes to its phones and laptops. For now, though, if it's colourful AirPods you're after, you'll have to make do with the AirPods Max while waiting for the standard AirPods to go full retro. Alas, you might be waiting a while – perhaps even longer than it takes for the company to bring back the iPod.

French agency Bruno rebuilds HelloAssoâs brand identity with Franklin Gothic poster type, bold pictograms, and unstaged member portraits.

That growth broke the old corporate look. As Chief Brand Officer Charlie Tronche told The Brand Identity, one rigid system couldnât cover such distinct roles without confusing people about who was speaking. Partnering with French agency Bruno, the team dropped generic stock photos and built a parent identity anchored in everyday club life. Look at the leaf-green campaign poster first. Heavy white uppercase headlines declare âIT HASNâT GOT ANY BETTER FOR NON-PROFITS SINCE 1901,â nodding to Franceâs July 1901 freedom of association law, while the tight HelloAsso wordmark locks squarely into the bottom-left corner.

Bruno Co-founder BarthÃ©lÃ©my Chalvet grounded the typography in Morris Fuller Bentonâs Franklin Gothic, pulling cues from dense 1970s protest posters and newspapers meant to read from across the street. Black and white carries every core statement. On a stark poster layered over a weathered housing handbook, eight stacked uppercase descriptors fill the frame edge to edge, and the same compressed wordmark sits calmly over an open French book spread or across the back of an event T-shirt. It doesnât need ornamental badges to hold attention. In motion, two animated pieces translate Brunoâs âindividual within the collectiveâ idea into a portrait mosaic that assembles and splits cleanly so copy replaces a tile instead of covering a face. That rule keeps candid club portraits, like the sunlit member in a blue 1901 tee, completely unobstructed.

It has been revealed that to keep HelloAssoâs expanding offers legible without splintering the system, Bruno locked each branch into one formula: the wordmark, a chunky black pictogram, and the offer name. Printed directly above an archival photocopy of the 1901 law, theatre masks mark HelloAsso Culture, a running figure anchors HelloAsso Sport, and a cupped hand holding a heart identifies HelloAsso GÃ©nÃ©rositÃ©. Color splits those branches right away â green stays with the parent platform, lime yellow codes Sport, red-black-white drives Culture, and cream-and-ochre layouts pace numbered brochure spreads like the Sommaire. At live gatherings, pale blue GÃ©nÃ©rositÃ© and red Culture jerseys hang behind oversized white 3D letters spelling Hello, turning brand architecture into clubwear. Everything lives inside an online brand book so HelloAssoâs internal teams can run the system on their own.

This cosy Godot-made indie game makes you feel like a still life artist

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you're looking for an antidote to the GTA 6 noise, Glenmara: Still Life Artist is it.
  • According to recent reports, despite the title, it's also not a painting game like, say, Mario Paint, but rather a simulation.
  • Instead, it's about being given objects you can assemble and position, then choosing filters and styles with the available tools and letting the game render it for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you're looking for an antidote to the GTA 6 noise, Glenmara: Still Life Artist is it. Think of still life art, and chances are an oil painting of fruit in a bowl or flowers in a vase. While you may be presented with those options in Glenmara, this casual, cosy game from four-person Dundee-based indie studio Bit Loom Games also lets you get creatively weird with more contemporary objects and styles.

According to recent reports, despite the title, it's also not a painting game like, say, Mario Paint, but rather a simulation. "It's just this small idea based on being interested in how scenes are composed," artist Caitlin Smith tells me.

Instead, it's about being given objects you can assemble and position, then choosing filters and styles with the available tools and letting the game render it for you. Artist Douglas Flinders adds, "The thinking there is you are playing the role of a competent artist, so the player has access to nice painting styles. It's like you don't need to be able to triple-jump in real life to do it in Mario. You get to feel that fantasy without necessarily needing the inherent skill yourself.".

Even though you are technically painting on a canvas, the filters you have available aren't limited to painting styles. Sure, you can use traditional oil paints or watercolours, but you can also opt for mosaic or styles that resemble cel-shading or pixel art. Being free to break from conventional expectations has been an notable design decision.

Recent findings suggest that "The [initial] idea was that you could be scored on how well you compose a theme with traditional rules, but it changed pretty rapidly after we realised it would just be much more fun to not have any rules and basically be able to do whatever you want creatively," Smith explains. "It was important to us to not have any sort of failed state. So if you want to sort of make this niche for yourself as a painter that puts eggs in all of your paintings, the game is not going to tell you you can't do that.".

As the team's first game made with the open-source engine Godot, which only launched its own asset store earlier this year, all of Glenmara's shaders for its different art styles were created from scratch by programmer Henry Pullan.

Recent findings suggest that "Coming to Godot from Unity, the image processing pipeline we were used to just wasn't there, and we had to come up with a different way of getting all the data to and from the GPU at the right time," Pullan explains. "Fortunately, they're not real-time effects, and being able to process the image over a few frames lets us really easily experiment.".

In a recent development, "This led to a system where we can stack effects on top of each other to create pretty different outcomes. The majority of the effects are using the library of shaders we've built up in different combinations to create a variety of effects.".

While playing as a newcomer to the fictional Scottish island of Glenmara might have you thinking of the premise of other cosy games like Animal Crossing: New Horizons, the inspiration is closer to home for Bit Loom's members, who all grew up in small places, including one from Jersey in the Channel Islands.

"We're going for the small-knit community part of Scotland where everyone kind of knows each other," notes Smith. "We tried to put this in the game in various ways, including character dialects, topics of conversation, your object collection and certain events that feature in the narrative. We hope that all of these things can work together to create a comforting, homely feel for players, and even a nostalgic one for some.".

This also means avoiding the trap of turning the game into a cosy capitalist sim where your still-life art is your side hustle, and you're incentivised to earn money from commissions to unlock more content.

"It would restrict creativity, and we just want people to go crazy and do loads of cool stuff in a painting," states Flinders. "Also, the story we want to tell and the feeling you get throughout is a lot more about making these pieces of artwork as gifts for members of your community that you're getting to know in a new place you've moved to. You're forming relationships with these people.".

Glenmara: Still Life Artist is coming soon to PC, and you can wishlist it on Steam.

In a recent development, alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

#80443. Latest Update: Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year confirmed

Latest Update: Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year confirmed

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An old sailor’s home that pays homage to its nautical heritage has won Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year following the announcement of all 14 interiors category winners at a party in London.
  • The 14 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme are located in 10 different countries, including Australia, China, Czech Republic, Kazakhstan, Mexico and Ukraine.
  • Industry observers note that la Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects won the interiors project of the year award, sponsored by Gaggenau.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An old sailor’s home that pays homage to its nautical heritage has won Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year following the announcement of all 14 interiors category winners at a party in London.

The 14 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme are located in 10 different countries, including Australia, China, Czech Republic, Kazakhstan, Mexico and Ukraine.

Industry observers note that la Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects won the interiors project of the year award, sponsored by Gaggenau. It was also named residential interior (small) project of the year.

“This was probably the boldest and most well-executed project we saw,” said the judges.

“They kept everything that was already there and made a much more interesting place,” adding that, “it’s very well-thought-out in terms of how space has been used.”.

La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects.

The winning project of the year was up against category winners, including a restaurant that features “direct and unrefined” materials to create tactile interior in Canada, a pink stepped-facade-fronted commercial building and interiors in Mexico and a boutique that recalls a traditional yurt in Kazakhstan.

A boutique hotel in Bali focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture and a warehouse into a workspace divided by glass partitions and filled with design classics, including an entire Jean Prouvé house were also amongst the category winners.

Read more about all the winning interiors projects below:.

Interiors project of the year and residential interior (small) of the year: La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects.

The Spanish practice renovated the home in Mataro, Spain, which belonged to a sailor in the 19th century, updating its interiors to suit the lifestyle of his descendant, who lives there now.

There was no discussion – this was the winner.

The project saw the renovation of three spaces: the entrance hall, the dining room and the living area. The judges praised the project’s bold approach, noting there was no deliberation over its winning credentials: “There was no discussion – this was the winner.”.

“It’s super unusual,” they continued, “and we liked to see an intervention in a very historical space where they decided to not play it safe.”.

Residential interior (large) of the year: Garden Home by Gisbert Pöppler.

Local studio Gisbert Pöppler won residential interior (large) of the year for its renovation of a 1920s villa in Ruhr, Germany.

For this project, we were swayed by the colours and use of materials, as well as the contrast between the very classic exterior of the house and its interior.

The interior design features a bold colour scheme and artisanal details that reflect its association with the Deutscher Werkbund movement, which caught the judges’ eyes.

“For this project, we were swayed by the colours and use of materials, as well as the contrast between the very classic exterior of the house and its interior,” they stated.

“It has character and doesn’t play it safe,” they continued.

Restaurant interior of the year: Jeju by &Daughters.

Canadian studio &Daughters won restaurant interior of the year for Jeju, a Korean restaurant in Vancouver, Canada.

This project has a level of innovation while being quite exquisite in every element.

A rich material palette of basalt, cork, concrete, thatch and wood characterises the restaurant interior, which nods to traditional touches in its contemporary design.

In a recent development, “This project has a level of innovation while being quite exquisite in every element,” the master jury stated. “It’s contemporary and still a bit traditional. There’s also a cultural influence that’s being used well and isn’t just there for decoration.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Bar and cafe interior of the year: Laibei 1087 by Tant A Temps Design.

Laibei 1087 by Tant A Temps Design in Xi’an, China, won bar and cafe interior of the year, sponsored by Programa.

There are a lot of beautiful projects, but this one is really refreshing – it’s working with the building, but also reinventing it.

Located inside the Beilin Museum, the cafe’s interior aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty and used a minimal intervention renovation strategy with every new addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.

“This project is new and modern, but still connected to the past,” the judges mentioned.

“There are a lot of beautiful projects, but this one is really refreshing – it’s working with the building, but also reinventing it.”.

“The architect has taken symbolic elements and simplified them, which makes it feel quite fresh.”.

Hotel and short-stay interior of the year: Moon Gang by YSG Studio.

Australian studio YSG won hotel and short-stay interior of the year for its conversion of a former private vacation residence into a boutique hotel in Bali, Indonesia.

There’s a lot of innovation and playfulness here, and a good use of local craftsmanship, as well as a collaborative spirit.

Focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture, Moon Gang Bali hotel is located among the rice fields on the northern outskirts of Ubud and includes five interconnected suites, outdoor terraces and a lounge surrounding a central courtyard.

YSG was influenced by Indonesian and Japanese design for the hotel’s spaces, which feature bamboo and timber structures and lava stone tiling.

“There’s a lot of innovation and playfulness here, and a good use of local craftsmanship, as well as a collaborative spirit,” commended the master jury.

Workplace interior (small) of the year: Rosadoce by Reims 502.

Rosadoce by Reims 502 in Querétaro, Mexico won workplace interior (small) of the year, sponsored by Framery.

This is a very architectural project, but that architecture has influenced the interior.

Featuring a stepped facade, the commercial building’s pink characterises the warm feel of the interior, being used throughout the workplace with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone.

“This is a very architectural project, but that architecture has influenced the interior,” noted the master jury.

“We like how they connected the interior and exterior design,” they continued, “it’s an adaptable and very sophisticated design.”.

Workplace interior (large) of the year: Not A Hotel Office by Not A Hotel.

Not a Hotel’s own office in Tokyo, Japan won workplace interior (large) of the year, sponsored by Framery.

We found this one very impressive; it was quite radical and dramatic.

The Japanese hospitality manufacturer’s in-house architecture team turned a 1967 warehouse into a workspace featuring a brutalist design divided by glass partitions and a spacious interior with seven-metre-tall ceilings.

“We found this one very impressive; it was quite radical and dramatic,” said the judges.

“It really makes coming to the office feel like a dip back into the culture.”.

Retail interior (small) of the year: Gunia Project Showroom by Temp Project.

Local studio Temp Project won retail interior (small) of the year for its lifestyle store in Kyiv, Ukraine.

The mix between the old and new is very interesting.

Modern materials, including mirrors and tiled surfaces, were used to complement the building’s original ornate interior for brand Gunia Project, which occupies the ground floor of a late 19th-century building located on a historic street near Kyiv’s Golden Gate.

“The mix between the old and new is very interesting,” said the judges.

“It must have been a constraining space to work in,” they observed, “but the end result feels very carefully edited and sophisticated.”.

Retail interior (large) of the year: Messa House by Up2date.

Up2date Architects won retail interior (large) of the year for the minimalist Messa House store in Almaty, Kazakhstan.

Beige interiors are boring unless they’re done well and for this one, the use of material is just perfect.

Commissioned for womenswear brand Messa, the 350-square-metre store was designed to reimagine the form of a Kazakh yurt, with breakout areas and an on-site cafe.

“Beige interiors are boring unless they’re done well and for this one, the use of material is just perfect,” praised the master jury.

The judges also commended “the contrast between the glossy tiles, wall and furniture”.

“It’s like a small architectural world inside the space,” they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Leisure and wellness interior of the year: Unravel by Atelier Write.

Japanese studio Atelier Write won the leisure and wellness interior of the year for its hair salon project in Tokyo, Japan.

This is a really good use of space – it’s very clever how they have integrated something that you wouldn’t imagine would fit in there.

Named Unravel, the project transformed a warehouse with statement features such as suspending mirrors, shelves and curtains from a series of industrial rails that allow the entire space to be reconfigured.

“This is a really good use of space – it’s very clever how they have integrated something that you wouldn’t imagine would fit in there,” noted the judges.

“It’s an innovative, moveable space and the movement has purpose; it’s not just a gimmick.”.

Exhibition design (interior) of the year: Life Behind the Walls by B² Architecture.

B2 Architecture won exhibition design (interior) of the year for its Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, Czech Republic.

They have used the materials that everyone uses for exhibition design, but in a latest way.

Using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea, the 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

“In this project, the colours black, white and red are used really well in a graphical way,” noted the master jury.

The judges also noted its material sensitivity, noting how surprising “the designers use soft materials to create emotions,” adding that “there’s a contrast between the technology and the use of textiles”.

“They have used the materials that everyone uses for exhibition design, but in a new way,” they added.

Kitchen interior of the year: Pine Island Cottage by Thom Fougere Studio & Bureau Tempo.

Canadian studios Bureau Tempo and Thom Fougere won kitchen interior of the year for Pine Island Cottage in Ontario, Canada.

You can imagine being there – washing the dishes with that view, you’d actually want to do them.

The getaway retreat’s materials are informed by the rocky surroundings of the host island in Ontario’s Georgian Bay.

“This kitchen is very functional and well laid out, but it’s also super beautiful and we like that they used local materials,” remarked the master jury.

“You can imagine being there – washing the dishes with that view, you’d actually want to do them.”.

Bathroom interior of the year: Lumeah by Pepper & Well.

Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well won bathroom interior of the year for Lumeah in Macedon, Australia.

We really liked the use of materials in this bathroom, with its mix of concrete, stone and glass.

The studio took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing the latest en-suite within one of the most intact examples of residential work by celebrated architect Paul Couch.

“We really liked the use of materials in this bathroom, with its mix of concrete, stone and glass,” stated the judges.

“The studio did a good job of creating a contemporary interior in a historic building, and we enjoyed how the bathroom feels like it continues out into the garden.”.

Sustainable interior of the year: Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo Design Studio.

Chinese studio RooMoo won sustainable interior of the year for Cloudhaus Hotel in Chongqing, China.

This is a great effort and if you want to be sustainable, it’s really well done.

RooMoo transformed a five-level former sales office into the Cloudhaus Hotel, retaining the building’s original structure while incorporating materials collected from the surrounding landscape and nearby villages.

Concrete drill cores, discarded bricks and timber salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins were repurposed for the 24-room retreat for its renovation, which the judges noted for being well-documented.

“This is a great effort and if you want to be sustainable, it’s really well done,” the master jury mentioned.

“They took a dark, concrete space and turned it into a warm interior through the use of wood, while keeping a lot of the existing materials,” they continued.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that how do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world?
  • In a recent development, while the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media.
  • Recent findings suggest that the data also indicates that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that how do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, demonstrates that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly important tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.

In a recent development, while the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report says.

Recent findings suggest that the data also indicates that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report indicates. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”.

Sources indicate that when it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents remarked they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).

A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.

Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also showed that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.

Sources indicate that the importance of ​​online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among new collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.

But can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.

It has been revealed that the report interestingly states that the youngest generation of collectors—Gen Z—are not the ones using social media the most in their collecting journeys. “The generation raised on social media is, it turns out, the one most inclined to keep its collecting close,” the report says. While the data indicated that Gen Z were the highest-spending generation surveyed and had the most wide-ranging collecting habits, their awareness of digital footprints leads them to seek greater control and privacy over their "personal and cultural identities".

According to recent reports, “Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”.

When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

Airline pricing is driven by demand, and demand follows predictable weekly patterns. Business travelers fly Monday mornings and Thursday or Friday afternoons. Leisure travelers fly Friday evenings and return Sunday afternoons. The days with the least demand — and therefore the lowest fares — are Tuesday, Wednesday, and Saturday.

Here is what the aggregate pricing data from Google Flights, Hopper, and airline fare databases consistently shows:.

Industry observers note that the savings are most pronounced on popular leisure routes (Fresh York to Miami, Chicago to Los Angeles, any route to Las Vegas or Orlando) where weekend demand is highest. On less popular routes or business-heavy corridors, the day-of-week effect is smaller. The practical takeaway: if you have any flexibility, fly out on Tuesday or Wednesday and return on a Tuesday or Wednesday. A couple flying round-trip can save $100 to $400 simply by shifting their travel days.

One important note: these are averages across thousands of routes. Individual route pricing varies based on competition, seasonal demand, and airline capacity decisions. Always compare specific dates using Google Flights rather than assuming Tuesday is cheapest for your exact itinerary.

It has been revealed that the old advice about booking flights on a specific day of the week — typically Tuesday at 1 AM — is a myth that has never been supported by data. Airlines use dynamic pricing algorithms that adjust fares thousands of times per day based on demand, competition, and remaining seat inventory. There is no magical booking day.

According to recent reports, what does matter is how far in advance you book. Here are the optimal booking windows based on aggregate data from Hopper, Google Flights, and CheapAir analyses of millions of fares:.

The general pattern is that prices start high when flights first open (9-11 months out), drop to their lowest point in the 1-3 month window as airlines compete for bookings, then spike in the final 2-3 weeks as remaining seats become scarce. Holiday travel follows a compressed version of this pattern with higher floor prices throughout.

The most reliable strategy is not to try timing the absolute bottom but to set fare alerts and buy when the price drops to a level you consider a good deal. Waiting for a slightly lower fare risks watching prices climb permanently as departure approaches.

It has been revealed that the right tools eliminate the need to manually check prices. Here is what works best and how to use each one:.

According to recent reports, fare alerts are the single most effective strategy for the time-constrained FI-minded traveler. Set alerts on Google Flights for every trip you are considering in the next 6 months. You will receive email notifications when prices drop, and you can book immediately without daily searching. This passive approach consistently saves $50 to $300 per ticket.

In a recent development, for those building a travel rewards strategy, credit card travel portals (Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Travel, Capital One Travel) sometimes offer slightly better prices than booking direct. More importantly, points earned through everyday spending can cover flights entirely. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into 50,000 points — enough for 1-2 round-trip domestic flights. The FI approach to travel rewards is not to spend more to earn points, but to redirect spending you would do anyway through a rewards-earning card and let the points accumulate passively.

The single biggest predictor of cheap airfare is not when you book or which tool you use — it is how flexible you are with dates and destinations. Google Flights date grid and Skyscanner everywhere search exist specifically to help flexible travelers find the cheapest options. Being willing to fly on a Tuesday instead of a Friday, or to visit Portugal instead of France, routinely saves 30-50% compared to fixed-date, fixed-destination searches. For FI-minded travelers, flexibility is a skill that pays dividends on every trip.

What matters is booking within the optimal window (1-3 months out for domestic flights) and setting fare alerts to catch price drops.

Recent findings suggest that for domestic flights, 1 to 3 months before departure is the sweet spot. For international flights, 2 to 8 months is optimal. Holiday travel should be booked 2 to 4 months ahead. Booking too early (6+ months for domestic) or too late (under 2 weeks) typically results in higher prices.
