💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, “Driving at rush hour.
  • According to recent reports, the premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface.
  • According to recent reports, to help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, “Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. We’d come full circle: The bumper-to-bumper traffic that Miami, the city I once called home, is now notorious for — in no small part due to overdevelopment, climate change, and strained infrastructure — was being alleviated by a video game that keeps people at home, inside a simulation of the same city locked in time.

According to recent reports, the premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface. The game follows Lucía Caminos and Jason Duval in the criminal underworld of Leonida, a fictionalized state based on South Florida: Miami becomes Vice City, the Everglades are the Grassrivers. But its portrayal of real-life hardships, socioeconomic inequality, and even Lucía and Jason’s love story, among other elements, has elicited deeper reflections and responses across our increasingly blurred online and physical worlds.

According to recent reports, to help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire. Castañeda is an artist and video game designer exploring Latin American Surrealism in the digital age, and soto co-leads Artists for Artists: Miami, which is leading a boycott of Art Basel next month, and works in the overlapping arenas of labor rights, public infrastructure, and conceptual and social practice.

It has been revealed that our conversation was edited and condensed for clarity. I hope you enjoy it.

Sources indicate that left: Leo Castañeda playing GTA VI, with a mural by Ahol Sniffs Glue included in the game. Right: misael soto's selfie in front of the inside of the clock tower in Assisi (photos courtesy the artists).

Recent findings suggest that hyperallergic: Before we even get into GTA, I was hoping each of you could tell me a little bit about your relationship to Miami — how long you've been there? How do you feel about living there now?

Leo Castañeda: I moved to Miami first when I was 11. My parents first moved to Fresh York [from Colombia], and then they thought it was too cold, so they moved to Miami. I went to middle school and high school here, then I moved to New York for college, and I moved back in 2015. When I first moved back after college, it was mostly because of the cost of living in New York. And then, within the 10 years that I've been here, it became the same cost of living as New York, except with Florida salaries.

I do feel grateful, though, to be part of the Bakehouse Art Complex, where I have an affordable studio. I live in the North Beach area, and I was able to find a sustainable rent. Miami has a lot of arts nonprofits that help over time. I do feel that, as complicated as the Miami arts ecosystem is, it is pretty supportive — but at the same time, it is tied to all the different layers of money that have come in and dominate the arts, which are very present here.

Industry observers note that misael soto: I moved here right after undergrad. I grew up in South Florida, originally from Puerto Rico, and Miami was always la locura, down south. We would visit my cousins and whatnot from time to time. As I became more and more interested in starting my own practice, I moved down here and have continually been sucked back in. I try to leave, and it pulls me back for whatever reason. Since COVID, everything's changed. Miami became the second most expensive city in the country. The influx was palpable: All of a sudden, there were Texas and California and Upcoming York license plates, Teslas zipping around town, and rent just started skyrocketing. There's more flooding. But at the same time, it's gorgeous, and it's special. I live in Mid-Beach. I can go to the water, I can breathe in some sea air, I can hear 10 different languages at once.

In a recent development, it's a really complex relationship with Miami. Especially, I think, both of us make complicated art — we both make art that is unconventional and perhaps even, you could say, difficult to collect. I don't know if you describe yourself that way, Leo, but I definitely do. And making this kind of work in a hyper market-driven neoliberal city like Miami, on the one hand, it gives me a lot of fodder, a lot of material, a lot of things to talk about, as we're doing right now. But at the same time, it can be really frustrating and alienating and lonesome, ultimately.

H: I moved from Argentina to Miami when I was little because my mom got a job there. We lived in the Doral neighborhood, where most people I knew were also from Latin America, until I left for Chicago for college at 18. I've lived in Newly introduced York for over a decade now, but I still feel a strong pull to Miami, I feel seen, surrounded by people whose identities are a bit fractured the way I feel mine is.

Sources indicate that and on the note of nostalgia, GTA is a game that was made over the last 13 years, so it chronicles a Miami that’s partly gone. For example, people say Lucía's home is based on a cute salmon-pink, 13-unit condo in Edgewater that was demolished in 2022 to build a 55-story tower, yet it lives on in the game. What does it mean for a video game to preserve a place that no longer exists?

Recent findings suggest that LC: Well, a few thoughts. During that 13-year development, I would assume the map design was one of the first things they did. But there are also aspects of the chronicling of Miami, or Miami becoming this satire through the game, that have evolved in a shorter time period. For example, this morning I woke up, and there was a Miami Instagram influencer saying that in the fictional version of the Cuban coffee shop Versailles, which is called Antoinette, the bakery has a sign posted outside that states something like, “any politician must pay for all the food when they leave.” That's a reference from a few years ago, when Trump reportedly went to Versailles, ordered food for everyone, and then didn't pay and just walked out.

According to recent reports, so it does seem like a video game takes a long time to make, and this one is probably the most ambitious one ever made — 4,500 people working really, really hard, to the point of even having the union situations that they have in the UK branch of the company. But at the same time, I feel like they studied Miami extremely well, and the integration with some local businesses and local artists in particular — I've seen a few street artists like Ahol Sniffs Glue, Soak, Tatiana Suarez, Typoe, as well as musician Nick León. One restaurant is based on Juvia on Lincoln Road, which doesn't exist anymore — they got priced out, and now there's a record of it. The game takes so long to make, but it lives in an ever-present, because it doesn't matter if you made an asset 13 years in the past, like Lucía's apartment, or now; they feel like the present. It's an interesting amalgamation. I would have to spend more time with it to really know: Does this feel like Miami in 2014 or Miami in 2026, or a hybrid?

H: To get into the politics of the conversation around GTA, I have a lot of icky feelings about one narrative that's taking hold online, which is that the game is “Woke 3.0,” and that the incels and Trump supporters are pissed about it. I only played for a few hours last night, and I went into a gun shop and bought a shotgun. That, to me, panders much more to the NRA hawks and the pro-gun community than to anything that could be considered woke, you know?

MS: Hmm. I see it the other way around, actually. To me, it's like pretending in order to pacify, in some ways. It's a very complex thing. On the one hand, I remember seeing the woman twerking on the top of a car as the sun came up over the MacArthur. Now that's in the game. And I remember the “face eater” on the MacArthur. I see a man in a thong skateboarding weekly, and now there's a character like that in the game. I teach art history, and I do a whole week on postmodernism and poststructuralism and simulacrum, and the consequences of that, which I think have led us into some really dangerous flattening territory in terms of the role of the artist in the late 20th to early 21st century. I see this game and the way that it's taken over the city in real life and in gameplay, and it makes me think about how much of this is pacifying the role of the artist, or is it pushing through to the other end and becoming a meta-modernist critique that has some gems in there, if you're willing to find them?

Industry observers note that it ultimately makes me feel a bit sad in terms of what we deserve. I texted you yesterday, Valentina, when we were talking about having this conversation, and I noted, “Well, maybe this is the kind of art the city deserves.” It's not the art that I want for Miami. But in so many ways, Miami is the perfect place. It's been the city for continual use by image makers, from Hollywood to video games.

H: There is some talk about the fact that the game does seem to have an awareness and sensitivity around identity. Cygnus, the curator at the Vice City Museum of Art, is the first non-binary character in Grand Theft Auto history. The actor cast for the role, Jesse James Rose, said that to prevent anti-trans violence, GTA made it so players would not be able to harm their character. Does this feel like an honest gesture, though?

Industry observers note that MS: I was just talking to a friend who's been playing it, and she was like, “Where are all the Haitians?” I remembered there was this huge lawsuit against GTA and Vice City, the one set in the ’80s, from about 20 years ago. Haitian groups sued Rockstar over their portrayal. I did some research, and it seems now the firm has shifted. They're saying, “We now punch up as opposed to punching down.” That feels, once again, so uncanny in comparison to the ways in which corporate America has shifted. It makes me think of the phrase, “Black faces in high places won't save us.” I don't want to be lobbing grenades at Rockstar. I think it's fantastic that these changes have been made, especially with such an influential game. But at the same time, it feels like the video game, in its attempt to replicate reality, is lagging in this area.

H: GTA has a long history of racism. We shouldn't forget that Black characters have been associated with criminality throughout all editions of the game. I haven't played enough to say whether that's the case in the latest version. There is also the question of how the organization actually treats its workers, and the labor disputes that are going on behind the scenes. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer for Rockstar, wrote an opinion piece for the Guardian where he asked, why is it that with this game that generated billions of dollars, we are still fighting to get union recognition?

MS: I'm curious, Leo, as someone who has been playing games for as long as you have, how you feel about this. I'm a cinephile — I've been one since I was 18, and watched my first Kubrick film the summer before college. And I am dying to see Avengers: Doomsday (2026). I've been following the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) and have been consistently floored by the way they built out this world and the interconnected films. It's history, and it's been making history. But we all know how terrible Disney is. And even with the MCU, they tried to bring in more diversity, and the public didn't respond, so they backtracked on it. I don't know if that analogy holds. But it feels pertinent. It feels similar.

LC: Of course, I have to play more to fully understand it. There's the ads of the game and the game itself. I would say that the Netflix special did feel like it was perpetuating some of the stereotypes of the Haitian community. But at the same time, having played, or seen the range of minority characters so far in the first couple hours, it feels like they have a wide range of personalities, body types, and interests. It's not like they're all criminals. And I also found out that local Haitian muralist Serge Toussaint has his work featured in the game, which I think is an amazing thing. But in terms of artworks in other mediums that really relate to this, this is kind of like, let's say, South Park, or Euphoria — reveals that are a mirror to the world that's very explicitly showing you both the best and the worst, and it's making fun of and critiquing everyone. But then how does it flip to show a upcoming perspective or a solution?

Recent findings suggest that I've seen a lot of people, especially women game critics and game developers, celebrating the relationship of Jason and Lucía being a central situation in the game, as opposed to a cast of different men from different backgrounds, or, in GTA IV, the Eastern European guy in the seedy underground. Having the relationship and the cultivating of the relationship be a core mechanic, almost in a Sims-like way — and even the learning of emotional labor, or doing kind things around the house, or the game having a really interesting reward mechanic for the nonviolent interactions ... At least in my experience so far, three hours in, I haven't shot a single shot.

H: Wait, how did you save Donnie in the first mission without shooting people?

Industry observers note that LC: Oh, by hiding. It was saying, “Crouch around to make sure no one sees you.”.

It has been revealed that H: I think it's fascinating how different players can make these different decisions. I'm not very good at gaming, so I gave my husband the controller. I was like, “Get us out of here as quickly as possible. I want to get to Vice City!”.

Industry observers note that LC: Yeah, and usually my criticism of Rockstar Games and also Naughty Dog, two big companies that have these cinematic, movie-like games, is that the story missions often have a path where you fail if you don't take a violent action. The emergent gameplay — which happens just by walking around, the dynamic gameplay that's not in a story mission — is usually extremely layered and nuanced and can go in any direction, violent or not. Again, I'm only three hours in with GTA VI, but so far I appreciate that it is giving the choice of not using violence, and kind of rewarding it. There's something interesting about that. Because usually in those Rockstar games, I'm like, okay, there's this emotional tale, and now there's a mission, and I have to kill 20 minions.

It has been revealed that MS: Leo, I'm thinking about your work and playing your pieces, immersing oneself in these worlds that you create, and there's a kind of mystery in the expansive potential that you create in your installations that at first can be a little overwhelming, but you have to just dive in. And this is the nature of games, or video games. There's a kind of trust fall. And I'm thinking about — let's just go there — the emancipatory potential of that. Because video games, to me, the potential in them as works is the building of awareness, the fostering of empathy, literally embodying someone who has a different way of life or a different body, a different perspective. Especially in our era of political correctness, and a lot of it is warranted, we're asked to speak from our own perspective and not assume things of others. And so this allowance — I wonder how you see the potential in that, especially in something like this game that is so immersive.

LC: I think games as artworks are, to a certain extent, some of the most affordably accessible. Yes, you need to have a PC or PlayStation or Switch or something, but they could be pieces of art that are globally accessible in an immediate way, and they really can affect culture. In terms of empathy, you're controlling a being that you identify as “I”: “I” drove the boat today, or in my game, “I” was camouflaging with the environment to gain energy. There's something there about the mutability of the body, or how one could shift one's self-identity into multiple beings, that is interesting in games, and also interaction and choice as a place that could be art, in a way that performance art also does, and maybe theater. And visual arts in general, maybe in a less touch-based way. But in terms of the empathy, I've been seeing a lot of reviews of GTA VI saying it's actually leading people towards that. Perhaps it is through the romantic relationship [between Jason and Lucía], or maybe by having so much freedom to do whatever you want and kill whoever you want, but then developing these characters and NPCs to a level where they feel like real people.

H: There is one moment in the game that was very emotive in a way that might provoke empathy, and it certainly did for me. At the very beginning — so this is not really a spoiler — we're shown the backstory of how Lucía gets arrested. She's been sitting at a cafe, a little Cuban cafecito, and she's just ordering ice water. The server keeps coming up to her and asking if she wants something else, and she's like, “No, no, just ice water for me.” It's clear that she just can't afford anything else. So in an act of true desperation, and from a place of deep poverty, she decides to rob a payday loan store nearby, and she gets caught. At one point, you can hear the cops saying, “She's saying she left something at the cafe.” And then we see the owners of the coffee shop taking care of her baby, who is then taken by social services.

We're not shown Tomás, her little baby, at the beginning. It's something that the game surprises us with. To me, it was such a thoughtfully articulated moment.

LC: The beginning is so strong. And then having the tutorial on how to walk and use the camera be her nine months later in prison. Out of overcapacity, the prison is letting some people who have lower sentences perhaps have probation, so she's gonna be let go, but the woman who works there notes she doesn't know if or when Lucía will see her baby again. That works as a narrative tool, a teleology, giving purpose to the game beyond, “Oh, she's just a digital girlfriend.” Now there's this question of what the rewards of behavior are that the game's gonna have when one is part of the criminal underworld, but there is a child in foster care that could be taken back or not. That's gonna be so interesting if that ends up being a fork in the road within the narrative, because many of these games have multiple endings.

MS: This is so fascinating to me in regards to something we were talking about earlier — whether reality is informing the simulacrum and vice versa. It makes me think of how, living in Miami, it continuously feels like maybe the most neoliberal city I've ever lived in. But in so many ways, it oftentimes feels like when you're on the road or when you're at a cafe, you're alone. You really have to fend for yourself in this city. Of course, there are these moments where you break through, or if you're a regular at Enriqueta's, you know who to talk to, this and that. It makes me wonder how the game might change the way that we see ourselves. And, following that thread, how might it actually make us more united?

I don't know if that's a bit of a stretch, but there are just so many people playing this game. And I think over time it's really going to show, as visitors come and reflect their years of gameplay back to the city. In the same way that folks experience Paris syndrome, what will the GTA Miami syndrome be? How might that change us? I was thinking about it for the worse, but how might it change us for the better? Because I don't know a Miami where that childcare situation in the GTA story would happen. Of course, I'm not a caregiver. I'm not a parent. But I don't know that Miami — and I've been here long enough and I have a lot of family here, chosen family. So that makes me, in a weird way, hopeful.

LC: I think it's interesting, let's say with Pop art and conceptual art — if you use a urinal or a fluorescent light, you think of urinal, Duchamp; fluorescent light, Dan Flavin, etc. These artists are claiming this thing from the world. And it's interesting to have this very fluid cycle of, let's say, the Only in Dade Instagram account becoming almost a live feed of GTA, or us within Miami filtering our experience — when there's a very special or odd moment, it being a rehearsal for the game, or the game getting reflected back in the world.

It has been revealed that if the game is marketing itself as this debauched, wild place, and that lures millions and millions of people in, but then it ends up being this profound story that actually shows how South Florida has issues of income inequality and climate change ... There's a hurricane system in the game, so there's a very strong chance that there will be flooding. Will that situation, where violence and comedy, or things that are not explicitly telling people what the values should be, actually make them more subtle and implicit? Does that create change or not?

Recent findings suggest that H: We've been speaking over an hour, we could probably talk for two more hours. This feels like a beautiful note to end on. But I want to ask if there are any burning observations you want to share.

MS: I feel like we should speak about the takeover of Miami in the real world, physically. Anybody trying to do anything — F1, Art Basel, all these people who come in and take over the city, as they've done for decades — if they want to gain favor with locals, just look at what they did with GTA. Because the amount of free advertising — I mean, I went to this GTA VI-themed drag night, and it was not sponsored by them. It was at Las Rosas. They had a pool table and some neons, and they had the beer from the game available for purchase, but the event itself was fully done just to hop on the bandwagon, and everybody was lapping it up. Morphine Love Dion was playing the video game while people were dancing. It layered some uncanny feelings for me. But at the same time, I'm just very, very impressed, and scared, by the power of putting it everywhere to the point where it was inescapable. It's been inescapable for the last week. It's very impressive.

LC: Yeah. I've met at least two or three people who have been working on some of the release parties. So they're employing local artists and local musicians and local businesses, as opposed to, as misael was saying, these people arriving out of nowhere, renting a place for really exaggerated prices, and not giving back to the local community. At least through employment. We'll see over time if and how it leads to other forms of sustainability locally. I have a photographer friend who, similarly to that drag show, started doing GTA-style photos in front of one of the fresh signs and probably made some money through that, unofficially. So that's interesting.

Sources indicate that MS: I think there's many ways to be a capitalist, or to do this kind of thing and take over the city in this way. And I've never seen something so thoughtful. It honestly reminds me to some degree of the first couple years of Art Basel, when they would do a lot of public programming and free concerts and they really seduced us ... But that's another conversation. I'll stop there.

H: Well, it's a perfect aperitif for Miami Art Week and the Basel boycott and everything else. And then the G20 summit hosted by Trump in Miami the following week.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the past couple of years, most of the press releases coming from software companies have contained announcements of fresh AI features.
  • Industry observers note that canva is one of those companies, and it's introduced a bunch of generative AI tools to its design platform.
  • Canva has added two AI controls for both Free and Pro users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the past couple of years, most of the press releases coming from software companies have contained announcements of fresh AI features. Image, video and vector generation, removal tools, agentic workflows, AI assistants, and myriad other advances that can help artists do in seconds something that used to take hours.

Industry observers note that canva is one of those companies, and it's introduced a bunch of generative AI tools to its design platform. So the email I received yesterday made me do a double take. On the day that Anthropic completed the world's biggest IPO in history, it introduced an 'AI off switch'.

Canva has added two AI controls for both Free and Pro users. The generative AI switch can be used to hide all of its generative AI tools, including Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Expand, Dream Lab and Canva Code. It can be switched on or off at any time.

Sources indicate that there's also an option to “See less AI content” on Canva's library of templates and design elements. This addresses complaints about the glut of AI-generated content making it harder to find quality work, something that's been causing problems on platforms as varied as Etsy and ArtStation.

It has been revealed that canva claims AI-generated content remains a "small portion" of its library and that such content is identified in its metadata. Turning on the latest function isn't guaranteed to remove it completely, but it should put human-made templates and design elements first in search results and recommendations.

It has been revealed that the addition of a couple of toggles to the UI wouldn't normally be breaking news, so the fact that Canva feels this deserved its own announcement is telling. After heavily promoting AI tools, it's now presenting the ability to turn them off as a groundbreaking advance – and it is. This might be the first time that a major AI-forward creative software developer has recognised that a sizable portion of its user base just isn't into it.

"We believe AI has extraordinary potential to help people bring their ideas to life, and we're excited to keep pushing the boundaries of what's possible," Canva says. "At the same time, like so many of you, we know there's something special about the time, care, and creativity that goes into making something that's truly yours.".

Industry observers note that an 'AI off button' is something that some creatives have been calling for. Part of the difficulty in implementing one is that it needs a definition of AI. Programs like Adobe's Photoshop have used machine learning for many years; it just wasn't branded as 'AI'. Many artists welcome tools that speed up their work, but not ones that do the creation part for them, especially if they're powered by models that were trained on unlicensed work.

It has been revealed that canva's recognised that. The toggle only turns off generative AI tools, such as ones that generate upcoming imagery, text or code from prompts. Assistive editing tools like Background Remover or Magic Grab, which lets you select and move an object in an image will still be available. Using them won't cause your work to be shamed with metadata identifying it as AI-generated.

Industry observers note that A 'no AI button' also requires a willingness from the provider. Since generative AI features are often charged on a per-use basis via credits, software companies generally want to encourage their customers to use them.

Adobe teased some impressive-looking AI-powered tools in the Adobe Max Sneaks presentation last week, but it's also clear that some customers detest generative AI, which has created a market for fresh tools like the artist-led Niva app, which is promoting itself as AI-free art software.

Will an AI-off button let Canva have its cake and eat it?

You can learn more about Canva on the website.

There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

Industry observers note that swimming in a Peter Bradley color field. Leaping from dot to dot on a Howardena Pindell speckled canvas. A Peter Jemison horse prances toward me. A Pepsi Cherry truck pulls over as I’m having deep thoughts about authenticity.

Industry observers note that in the morning glow, a pretty woman walks down the sidewalk with a carton of a dozen eggs. A faded black-and-white Marilyn Monroe poster greets customers at the Organic Deli. A photo in the paper demonstrates the presidents of the United States, China, and Russia against a giant painting of the Great Wall. A Madonna song whispers, “Express yourself, express yourself.”.

A well-dressed man cycling to work is nice to look at. A Hilma af Klint painting sells for $12.7 million at auction, 16 times its highest estimate. Meanwhile at the supermarket, just three small items set me back $100. How could that be? If the middle class had any guts, they’d be out there on the streets burning effigies of Adam Smith and Sigmund Freud. But they’re not; they’re waiting 40 minutes in line across the street just to buy a bagel.

At the Ace Hotel, I read something I’ve written for the new edition of The Other Almanac. I wear my heart on my sleeve in front of strangers. The next speaker is a whale necropsy expert. At the end of the evening someone is crowned “Squash King.”.

A golden sunset falls over the glass towers of Long Island City. The Kosciuszko Bridge is lit with cotton candy colors. Fog in Downtown Brooklyn, or is it smoke? I can’t really tell. In Chelsea, I follow a group of people into an art gallery just to see what they’re into. It turns out to be a massive mistake.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief.

In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Lucas Blair Simpson.

Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, USA, “breathing new life” into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.

According to recent reports, the project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns. It serves as a major transit hub for the Northeastern United States.

The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.

Keeping to the historic details, including the art deco chandeliers that hang from the tall ceilings, SOM restored the space with builder Gilbane through renovation and a series of specific interventions.

Chief among these was the moving of ticketing, bag drop-off, and other facilities that had been placed in the main train hall into a little-used northern wing of the building.

“Our restoration and repositioning presents an extraordinary opportunity to leverage the station’s strengths, while breathing latest life into this beloved building,” remarked SOM Partner Colin Koop.

This move freed up more room for seating and through traffic in the main hall.

Working with retail partner Nelson Worldwide, SOM also revamped the concessions in the south concourse.

SOM worked closely with US rail system operator Amtrak on the project, which includes offices for Amtrak in the upper levels of the building.

In a recent development, it is part of a wider renovation SOM declared for the station and surrounding areas in Philadelphia in 2016, which included a number of tall buildings. The status of these upcoming structures is unclear.

SOM noted the efforts in preserving the character of the structure.

“We are preserving its historic character while positioning the station for the next generation of travelers to come,” said SOM Principal Phil Wessell.

“As part of our broader work along Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor, this revitalization reinforces the station’s role as both a vital transportation hub and a defining civic space for Philadelphia.”.

SOM also led the renovation of Daniel Patrick Moynihan Train Hall in Newly introduced York in 2021, with plans for a Penn Station renovation released earlier this year by PAU.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that adobe software might still rule in many industries, but there's a growing number of alternatives, from Canva's free Affinity to open-source Krita, Maxon's Autograph for motion design and DaVinci Resolve for video editing. Into the fray, comes a fresh artist-led app who's main selling points include the fact that it DOESN'T have any generative AI tools.

NIVA is clean and light, works in your browser and it's led by a conceptual artist rather than a software developer. After it was announced on Instagram this week, it picked up close to 30,000 customers in 48 hours.

Like the recent AI-coded Adobe clones, NIVA was born out of a frustration with the direction of a certain Californian software giant. But it takes a very different approach. It wasn't vibe coded, and it doesn't attempt to replicate the look, feel or functions of any one existing program.

The project's led by Stuart Semple, an artist who previously annoyed Anish Kapoor by creating a very black shade of black.

"With Adobe pushing AI further into its tools, I wanted somewhere people could still practise their craft and make things themselves. No AI doing it for them," he states. "NIVA is very much our own thing that we've all built together.

Sources indicate that having previously made FREETONE, a free alternative to Pantone colours, with Culture Hustle, he started a Kickstarter for a project that was initially called Abode. He raised $240,000 from 3,000 backers, a few hundred of whom have been using the software regularly over a year and a half of beta testing. Around 10 people were involved more heavily in making the software, but Stuart indicates he largely built it himself "with help from some geeky friends from time to time when I've got stuck.".

Industry observers note that at some point the name changed, and the project became NIVA. "I can't say I woke up to a nasty letter from the lawyers representing Adobe for legal reasons, so I won't," Stuart comments.

It has been revealed that NIVA has many of the core tools and functionalities of a program like Photoshop. There are brushes, a pen tool with boolean ops, cloning and healing tools, layers, curve adjustments and blend modes, type tools with kerning, layouts and gradients.

Recent findings suggest that but it's lighter, with a more minimalist UI and fewer menus despite providing the ability to draw vectors, manipulate photos and lay out text and pages all in a single app. Users also get a portfolio page, and there's a visual asset library called Storehouse, where you can store, sort, search and share work. Work can be exported in formats including PDF and SVG.

The pricing model is refreshing too. There's no subscription, and NIVA is free to use for an hour a day. You can buy full-day passes for $10 a time, or you can buy permanent access for $100. If you buy a day pass and later go permanent, the price of the day pass will be discounted. This allows a full opportunity to try the software before committing.

The response so far has been more enthusiastic than Stuart ever imagined. "I'm so excited and a bit freaked out", he admits, adding that what he finds most encouraging is that over half of the people who used NIVA in those first 48 hours made something with it within 40 seconds of getting access.

"We're finally at a stage where it's stable enough and good enough to share with the world," he adds. It's only version one, the start of something I hope will be great. I still have loads I want to do with it".

You can use the software online at NIVA.design.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multiple heritage sites in Ukraine were damaged by Russian strikes on 19 and 20 November, including the Unesco-listed St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex and St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv, known for its frescoes, as well as 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa, the strategic port city on the Black Sea, which was hit a day earlier. The entire historic centre of Odesa was added to Unesco’s list of endangered World Heritage sites in 2023.

At least nine people were killed in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine during the hours-long attack on 20 November.

“Today, Russian drones damaged one of the most famous monuments of our country, the Volodymyr Cathedral,” Tetyana Berezhna, Ukraine’s deputy prime minister for humanitarian policy and minister of culture, wrote in a Facebook post on 19 November after the cathedral in Kyiv was hit, breaking windows and frames and causing “some damage to the paintings and structural elements”.

Sources indicate that the neo-Byzantine St Volodymyr Cathedral, built in the 19th century, is under the jurisdiction of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU), which broke with the Moscow Patriarchate and was granted autocephaly by Constantinople in 2018. Three of Russia’s most famous artists of the 19th century and early 20th century—Viktor Vasnetsov, Mikhail Vrubel and Mikhail Nesterov—created religious art for St Volodymyr’s, as did the Ukrainian artist Mykola Pymomenko, a teacher of Kazimir Malevich.

It has been revealed that the Austrian embassy, located next-door to St Volodymyr's Cathedral, was also damaged. Kyiv's municipal cultural heritage department published an inventory of damage from the attack, which also includes the embassy of the Netherlands.

A Russian drone was shot down over St Michael’s, which is the headquarters of the OCU, on 19 November.

Recent findings suggest that berezhna’s post cites the cumulative damage from Russia’s accelerating attacks: “Since the beginning of this year, the number of monuments damaged by Russia has increased by more than a third, and by the end of October it was almost 2,200. Almost 2,700 cultural institutions were also affected.”.

Sources indicate that the minister was in Lutsk, a historic city in northwestern Ukraine, this week to initiative for a conference marking the 600th anniversary in 2029 of the Congress of Lutsk, which brought together the regional monarchies of the time. A Russian strike on Lutsk in October damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, Cosmogony, a 2,000 sq. m work by the contemporary artist Petro Antyp.

In a recent development, unesco has condemned the latest attacks, especially on Odesa, “which hit the centre of the city, within the boundaries of the World Heritage property ‘The Historic Centre of Odesa’” and “reportedly caused damage to several heritage buildings, including the Kalio Palace, a monument of national importance,” according to a statement released by the organisation. The Kalio Palace, built in 1834, is attributed to the Swiss Italian architect Giorgio Torricelli.

The strikes came amid escalating tensions and a diplomatic chasm that appears to be widening. The Russian President Vladimir Putin said this week that the Kremlin would not negotiate any partial ceasefire or deal with Ukraine after it struck and incapacitated the Kerch Bridge linking mainland Russia to Crimea, a symbol of Russia’s annexation of the Black Sea peninsula in 2014, on 16 and 17 November. At the same time, US President Donald Trump claimed that peace, largely on Russia’s terms, is within reach and reportedly urged European leaders to stop funding weapons for Ukraine. Trump, Putin and the Chinese President Xi Jinping signed a “peace declaration” on 20 November at a trilateral summit hosted by Xi in Shenzhen, China.

Sources indicate that A petition to “safeguard Ukraine’s cultural heritage and artistic integrity” was launched last month by the curator Konstantin Akinsha and Bjorn Geldof, the artistic director at Kyiv’s PinchukArtCentre. It calls “for immediate sanctions and the suspension of Russian state participation in international cultural events”. Rapporteur, a Brussels-based policy publication, reported this week that ten European countries are seeking to keep Russia out of the 2027 Architecture Biennale. Russia’s participation in the 2026 Venice Biennale set off a series of protests.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Paul Dussault.

A dedicated space for preparing tea has been placed at the heart of this Canadian house’s renovated kitchen, designed by local studio Perron.

Perron overhauled the kitchen for a longstanding client, with whom the studio has worked on several professional and personal projects over the years.

Her residence sits along the south shore of the St Lawrence River, overlooking Quebec City on the opposite bank.

The view across the water, and the client’s love of tea, were the primary guiding elements for the renovation project.

“For this house, we were not simply working from a checklist of requirements,” remarked Perron founder Nathalie Perron.

“We already knew about our client’s lifestyle, energy and the things that are most important to her.”.

The kitchen space was divided into three zones: a space for tea, a central cooking area and a counter overlooking the river.

At the entrance, a small counter wrapped in glossy oxblood red tiles and a partition of burgundy steel bars form a niche that the client has nicknamed her “teahouse”.

Custom lacquered MDF wall shelves store and display cups, saucers, mugs and teapots that she has collected during her travels over the years.

“Each one evokes a specific memory and now has a place in her daily life,” said Perron.

An on-demand hot water tap is also installed within this niche, creating a dedicated space for the tea-making ritual.

The main kitchen area revolves around an angular island, which has space for a bar stool and incorporates a built-in electric stove.

Above, a cylindrical burgundy-hued range hood is framed within more steel bars, suspended from the ceiling to support shelves.

Rows of glass blocks are stacked between the upper and lower cabinets, which are both faced in stained white oak.

Ultra-thin steel shelves hang from the upper millwork, adding extra storage without blocking the light through the translucent bricks.

Opposite, a long counter faces the river through a large window, allowing the homeowner to witness passing ships and changing light conditions as she stands working or washing dishes.

Cristallo quartzite from Brazil forms the countertop and a backsplash.

Long, narrow Cotto Manetti terracotta tiles cover the floor, echoing the shapes of the matte and gloss pink Farblok ceramic tiles by Quintessenza that run up the wall in stripes.

A Mousse wall fixture by Quebec lighting brand JETA adds another feminine touch to the kitchen.

“It is a house that reflects a woman who enjoys going on adventures, but who has created a home that she loves returning to,” noted the studio.

Perron has offices in Montreal and Quebec, the latter in an early 20th-century building renovated to house a studio, showroom and Nathalie Perron’s home.

GTA 6's environmental storytelling is hidden in the details you might never notice

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best environmental storytelling in video games doesn’t always hit you in the face and demand you stop to look, and GTA 6 has perfected that.
  • Rockstar’s developers say that kind of discovery is central to Grand Theft Auto 6, a world designed to reward players who take their time.
  • Industry observers note that “The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto VI,” says Adam Cochrane, Vice President of Art: Environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best environmental storytelling in video games doesn’t always hit you in the face and demand you stop to look, and GTA 6 has perfected that. Sometimes it’s a carefully dressed room, an overgrown garden, or a detail you spot out of the corner of your eye while heading somewhere else.

Rockstar’s developers say that kind of discovery is central to Grand Theft Auto 6, a world designed to reward players who take their time. After three weeks of playing GTA 6, I'd say the world-building is some of the best, most detailed, and most nuanced I've experienced. It can be as small as mud on a character's trainers, a branded coffee mug, or a car decal.

Industry observers note that “The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto VI,” says Adam Cochrane, Vice President of Art: Environment. “The subtle sway of trees or bunting swaying in the wind. A puddle of bin juice around the bottom of a dumpster, or an overgrown garden in a property that is unoccupied.”.

In a recent development, it’s the sort of detail that makes a place feel inhabited rather than assembled for a game. Cochrane points to the personalisation of homes and businesses, and the little vignettes the teams have added for players to discover. Some offer in-game rewards; others are there simply to be found.

Industry observers note that “Then you zoom out, and you look at the sheer scale of the world, and you realise that the detail you’ve been discovering on such a small scale is quite literally everywhere across the vast landscape of this world,” he claims. “Then you realise that it’s all been curated, considered, and created by a human hand, and you can’t quite believe it.”.

Sources indicate that that thinking extends beyond what you can see. Steven Messinger, Senior Design Director: Open World, explains that Rockstar has built deep backstories for things players may only glimpse. The game’s gang compounds, for example, have a fully mapped drug network, from supply routes to street-level buyers.

“Players will only pick up on bits and pieces of this,” Messinger states, “but having that structure in the background as something we consistently refer to helps everything feel more real, like this massive machine is always running even when players aren’t there.”.

It’s a huge amount of work for details many players may miss. That’s rather the point.

15 Van Gogh Masterpieces that Set Auction Records

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1990 Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr.
  • Below are 15 of the Dutch master’s most remarkable paintings, each of which has achieved a place among the highest prices for a Van Gogh in auction history.
  • It has been revealed that A version of this article was first published on May 19, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1990 Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr. Gachet stunned the art world when it soared to $82.5 million at Christie’s Fresh York, setting a new record for any painting at auction at the time. It was one of several headline-grabbing sales that cemented Van Gogh as one of the market’s most coveted names. From swirling fields and blazing cypresses painted in Saint-Rémy to delicate still lifes and portraits from Arles and Auvers-sur-l’Oise, Van Gogh’s works continue to captivate collectors and institutions alike. Today his canvases routinely fetch eight-figure sums, driven by their emotional intensity and storied provenance.

Below are 15 of the Dutch master’s most remarkable paintings, each of which has achieved a place among the highest prices for a Van Gogh in auction history.

It has been revealed that A version of this article was first published on May 19, 2026. It was last updated on November 20, 2026.

On May 13, 2021, Christie’s New York auctioned Van Gogh’sBridge at Trinquetaille, completed in June 1888 during his productive Arles period. The painting achieved $37.4 million, including buyer’s premium, surpassing its pre-sale high estimate of $35 million. It depicts the road bridge to Trinquetaille across the Rhône River, near the house where Van Gogh lived for a time with Paul Gauguin. Notably, Van Gogh described the sky and river as “the color of absinthe,” a striking greenish yellow, reflecting his bold palette and emotional intensity. The scene includes figures that the painter called “ruffians of the Rue du bout d’Arles,” referencing the town’s red-light district. After his death, the painting passed through the hands of several owners, including his brother Theo, the British art collector Elizabeth Workman, and Saudi businessman Akram Ojjeh. The painting is right now held in a private collection.

This work from one of Van Gogh’s celebrated Sunflowers series of 1888 sold for approximately $39.9 million at Christie’s London on March 31, 1987, a record at the time for any painting sold at auction. The buyer was Yasuda Fire & Marine Insurance Co. of Japan (now Sompo), which donated the painting to the Sompo Museum of Art in Tokyo, where it remains today. Executed in vibrant yellows with expressive brushwork, the painting was created to decorate Van Gogh’s house in Arles before a visit by Paul Gauguin, symbolizing the artist’s optimism and creative aspirations during this fertile period in the South of France.

It has been revealed that this canvas, painted in 1890 during Van Gogh’s final months in Auvers-sur-Oise, depicts a seated woman against a backdrop of wheat stalks and poppies. The muted color palette and contemplative mood mark a departure from the artist’s earlier, more turbulent portraits. American casino magnate Stephen A. Wynn made news when he acquired the painting in 1997 for $47.8 million; in 2025 Wynn sold it privately, along with a painting by Paul Gaugin, to hedge fund manager Steven A. Cohen for a combined price of more than $100 million. These private transactions underscore Van Gogh’s enduring prominence and appeal in the art market, particularly for works from the last two years of his life.

On April 24, 1985, Van Gogh’s Landscape with Rising Sun, created in 1889 during his yearlong stay at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, sold for $9.9 million at Sotheby’s New York. This sale established a record for Impressionist and Post-Impressionist works, exceeding the previous Van Gogh auction high of $5.7 million. The painting portrays a wheat field in the early morning, viewed from the artist’s room on the first floor of the hospital. Before Florence J. Gould purchased it in 1965, the work was owned by physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, who inherited it from his father Julius, a Viennese collector. The painting was among the earliest Van Gogh works exhibited internationally and was part of the Museum of Modern Art’s first exhibition in 1929. Despite initial doubts about its market appeal, the sale underscored growing enthusiasm for Van Gogh’s landscapes and signaled a turning point in the valuation of his art.

Industry observers note that van Gogh’s Fields near Les Alpilles (1889) sold for $52 million at Christie’s in New York on May 12, 2022. Painted near the asylum at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, the work depicts a wheat field with lilac mountains behind it and a solitary almond tree in its center. The tree’s stark outline suggests Van Gogh’s admiration for Japanese prints. Until the sale, it had long been hidden in private collections, including that of it fashion designer Yves Saint Laurent and his partner Pierre Bergé, who had farmhouses near Saint-Rémy named after Van Gogh. It is rightly celebrated for its vivid brushwork and evocative colors capturing late autumn in the French countryside.

It has been revealed that on November 11, 1987, Sotheby’s Fresh York auctioned Irises, painted in May 1889 within days of Van Gogh’s voluntary admission to the Saint-Rémy-de-Provence asylum. The hammer dropped at $49 million, with a 10 percent commission bringing the total to $53.9 million. The winning bidder turned out to be Australian businessman Alan Bond, who was unable to complete the transaction. The painting was acquired for an undisclosed sum about three years later by the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles, where it remains today. Previously it had been in the collection of Joan Whitney Payson. Its bold colors and fluid brushwork mark a pivotal moment in Van Gogh’s artistic recovery, reflecting the emotional intensity and renewed vitality he found in nature during his time at the asylum. The dramatic sale drew a packed house and global media attention, cementing the ascendance of Van Gogh as a market titan.

Van Gogh’s Landscape Under a Stormy Sky was painted in April 1889 in Arles and sold for $54 million at Sotheby’s, Fresh York, on November 5, 2015. It was completed a few months after Van Gogh famously mutilated his ear in December 1888 and shortly before he admitted himself to the asylum at Saint-Rémy. The painting depicts a meadow filled with spring flowers, with a man and a woman walking on the left beneath heavy grey clouds. It was one of the last landscapes Van Gogh painted in Arles and is referred to in his letters to his brother Theo in mid-April 1889 as one of six spring studies. The canvas was later retrieved from Arles and sent to Theo in Paris in July. The sky, painted in thick expressive strokes, is unusual in Van Gogh’s Arles work and may reflect the difficult circumstances of his final months there.

Sources indicate that on November 4, 2014, Van Gogh’s Still Life, Vase with Daisies and Poppies, completed in June 1890 just weeks before his death, achieved $61.8 million at Sotheby’s New York, exceeding its estimate by over $10 million. The artist created this dramatic and colorful canvas while staying at the home of his physician, Dr. Paul Gachet. Garchet was an art collector and amateur painter, and Van Gogh is thought to have drawn inspiration from some of the works in the doctor’s house, including Cezanne’s flower paintings. He may even have given the still life in exchange for treatment.

In a recent development, this rare piece is one of the few Van Gogh paintings sold during his lifetime. It later entered the collection of Conger Goodyear, a founder of the Museum of Modern Art, before moving through private hands and being exhibited at the Albright Knox Art Gallery for over 30 years. The buyer was Chinese billionaire and entertainment mogul Wang Zhongjun, an amateur artist with a fondness for flower-filled compositions. This sale reflects a shift in the Van Gogh market, with East Asian collectors—especially in China.

Van Gogh’s The Avenue of Les Alyscamps was painted in November 1888 during his time in Arles, shortly after his friend Paul Gauguin came to stay with him. The work depicts in vibrant colors the central thoroughfare of the ancient Roman burial ground at Alyscamps, near Arles. It was created during a brief period of collaboration between the two artists, who captured the site, each from different viewpoints. After years in private collections, the painting was sold at Christie’s in New York on May 12, 2003, for $12 million. When it returned to auction at Sotheby’s New York on November 10, 2015, it fetched $66 million. The buyer was officially anonymous, though believed to be a Chinese collector. This dramatic increase reflects the continuing high demand for Van Gogh’s art.

Industry observers note that completed in 1889 at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, Wood Cabins Among the Olive Trees and Cypresses showcases Van Gogh’s distinctive impasto technique, depicting two modest buildings in vibrant natural surroundings. This pastoral scene reflects the artist’s deep connection to the Provençal landscape during his prolific asylum period. The painting fetched $71.35 million at Christie’s Newly introduced York on November 11, 2021, highlighting sustained collector enthusiasm for Van Gogh’s landscapes. Until then, it had been held in the collection of the Texas oilman Edwin Cox.

Recent findings suggest that painted in September 1889 at the asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, this work is one of the few self-portraits in which Van Gogh appears with no facial hair. Created shortly after he shaved his beard, it may have been intended as a gift for his mother to show that he was in better health. The intense blue-green background, combined with his direct, piercing gaze, gives the painting a raw emotional power that distinguishes the artist’s late works. Executed with his signature impasto technique, the canvas reflects both vulnerability and resolve during a fraught period in the artist’s life. It achieved $71.5 million at Christie’s New York in November 19, 1998. The work had previously been held in the collection of German entrepreneur Jacques Koerfer and was rarely exhibited, adding to its desirability.

In a recent development, painted in early September 1889 during Van Gogh’s stay at the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, Laborer in a Field features a lone peasant working beneath a vast, swirling sky. After a devastating epileptic episode that kept him away from painting for more than six weeks, Van Gogh returned to his brushes with renewed vigor and hope, using the view from his room—a wheat field enclosed by a stone wall—as inspiration. The painting’s earth tones and rhythmic brushwork capture not only its subject’s labor but also the artist’s own struggle toward creative and emotional renewal. This work, painted during one of the most turbulent yet fruitful periods of Van Gogh’s life, sold for $81.3 million at Christie’s New York on November 13, 2017, having passed through the estate of billionaire collectors Nancy Lee and Perry R. Bass. The painting’s return to the market after decades away attracted strong collector interest, reflecting both its artistic and historical significance.

Completed in Auvers-sur-Oise shortly before Van  Gogh’s death, Portrait of Dr. Gachet (1890) was hammered down for $82.5 million at Sotheby’s Upcoming York on May 16, 1990, setting a world auction record at the time. The buyer was Japanese businessman Ryoei Saito, who claimed he intended to have the painting cremated with him upon his death. This depiction of Dr. Paul Gachet, Van Gogh’s physician, shows him resting his head on one hand, surrounded by foxglove flowers and books. Its emotional intensity and the limited availability of works by the artist made it one of the most coveted Van Gogh portraits ever to appear on the market. After Saito’s death, in 1996, the painting’s whereabouts become uncertain. Reports suggest that it was sold to Austrian-born investment manager Wolfgang Flöttl in 1997 or 1998, but the current owner and location of the painting remain unknown.

Industry observers note that orchard with Cypresses (1888), painted during Van Gogh’s prolific Arles period, sold for $117.2 million at Christie’s New York on November 10, 2022, setting a record for the artist that still stands. The canvas portrays a vibrant Provençal landscape with twisting olive trees, dark cypresses, and a luminous sky rendered in thick, energetic brushstrokes. Before its record-breaking sale, the work was part of the collection owned by Paul G. Allen, the Microsoft cofounder. Its well-preserved condition, coupled with an exceptional provenance, contributed to its historic result at auction.

On November 18, 2026, Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), a picture of sunlit trees set against oncoming storm clouds, sold for $190.4 million (including fees) at Sotheby’s. The cover lot for the auction house’s Blaquier-Arrieta collection sale, which the house had billed as “legendary,” it set a new auction record for the Dutch painter. The reported buyer was dealer William Acquavella.

The artist’s previous record of $117.2 million was set at Christie’s in November 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888), a landscape from the collection of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen, sold for $102 million. The new result beat that by $73.2 million, a jump of 62.4 percent in just four years.

Recent findings suggest that that the sale happened at all was a victory for Sotheby’s. Just days before the auction, descendants of Samuel Fischer, the German Jewish publisher who once owned the painting, challenged its sale, arguing that their family had been forced to part with it in Amsterdam in 1936 because of Nazi persecution. Sotheby’s disputed the claim, pointing to archival records showing the painting had sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, around $22,000 at the time, which it considered a fair market price. After several days of talks, the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the Fischer heirs reached an agreement, clearing the painting’s title.

Painted shortly after Van Gogh arrived at Auvers-sur-Oise in May 1890, Blossoming Chestnut Trees is among the 70-plus paintings (and more than 50 drawings) that the artist made there before taking his own life only two months later. It was also one of only eight Auvers landscapes still in private hands, according to research cited by the Art Newspaper.

The electric scene, with its thick brushwork, also hadn’t been seen in decades. It was last exhibited at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in 1964 before Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro and Nelly Arrieta Blaquier, bought it in 1975—the kind of provenance and scarcity that fuels record-breaking prices like this one.—Daniel Cassady.

Latest Update: “We're not saying they're perfect” states architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its proposal to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers.
  • Revealed by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with fresh housing by 2051.
  • Officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Ben Hosking, Michael Pham.

Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its proposal to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers. In this interview, he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Revealed by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with fresh housing by 2051.

Officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.

But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has prompted concern from the UN’s special rapporteur on housing, and become a political issue in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.

Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice Office.

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility studies for keeping any of the condemned estates.

“We thought that was pretty odd that you wouldn’t do a refurbishment study on these estates,” Office director Simon Robinson told Dezeen.

“So we took it upon ourselves to start to do these feasibility studies, along with public housing residents.”.

“We’re not saying that they’re in perfect condition,” he added. “We’re also not saying that all of them should be refurbished – perhaps some are beyond repair. All we are saying is that these refurbishment studies need to occur.”.

In fact, feasibility studies have been conducted by the government but not been made public, despite requests by the Victorian Legislative Council.

By avoiding the relocation of residents, Office estimates that a retrofit and infill approach would cost around $300 million less than demolition and rebuild.

“As all the estates are occupied, the cost of relocating and housing the residents during construction work needs to be included in the project cost; this is consistently excluded and never disclosed,” said Robinson.

“We have estimated that these costs are very significant, with reports indicating that the government is spot purchasing or head-leasing properties from the private market.”.

The practice has put together a counter-proposal based on a strategy that it calls Retain Repair Reinvest (RRR).

RRR focuses on retaining buildings without displacing residents, carrying out renovation work to improve housing comfort and energy efficiency while reducing construction waste and carbon impact.

Recent findings suggest that robinson agrees that most of Victoria’s existing public housing buildings are right now not fit for purpose – buildings are rundown, cold in winter, and sweltering in summer. But he believes comfortable living standards can be achieved through renovations.

Office has applied its RRR strategy to three Melbourne estates in hypothetical case studies – Ascot Vale Estate, Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.

Formerly home to approximately 1,500 people, Flemington Estate’s four towers make up about 10 per cent of Victoria’s high-rise public housing stock.

Only about 32 households remain, though an injunction prevents Homes Victoria from serving further eviction notices while legal challenges are pending.

Office has proposed retaining the estate’s 720 dwellings and building an additional 577 infill social housing units to increase density.

Newly introduced facades and private balconies would be added, with other upgrades including integrated underground parking, a central communal green space, new heating and cooling systems, improved insulation, new kitchens and bathrooms.

Energy efficiency is another key focus. Double-glazed windows, photovoltaic cells, and water conservation systems would provide a 55 percent reduction of global warming potential compared to the demolition approach, according to Office.

Despite the seemingly obvious benefits, the Victorian government has so far been unmoved by the studies presented by the practice.

Robinson believes the reason lies in the fact that the state government no longer wants to manage public housing.

“When the state government manages public housing, they are responsible for maintaining the buildings and organising new tenants – all the admin that comes with owning a building,” he said.

As well as the demolitions, also attracting concern is the type of housing proposed for redevelopment under the HRRP.

Rather than like-for-like public housing, the fresh homes will be “community housing” – developed by private developers, and split between below-market and market-rate rental homes.

Despite still being classed as social housing by the state government, community housing is slightly more expensive, and the tenancy is less secure from eviction.

Robinson believes the term was created to misdirect the public.

“What they’re building is community housing, not public housing, so there’s no longer any public housing being rebuilt in Victoria,” he remarked.

“The government is now calling everything social housing, because they don’t want the public to know that it’s no longer public housing,” he continued.

“Victoria has the lowest percentage of public housing stock in Australia, and we’re right now demolishing it all and turning it into private and community housing.”.

The problem is particularly charged in the context of Australia‘s housing-affordability crisis. There are currently over 60,000 people on the waitlist for social housing in Victoria, where social housing accounts for three per cent of all dwellings, below the national average of 4.2 per cent and the OECD average of 7 per cent.

“Public housing serves as foundational social infrastructure that treats shelter as an essential human right,” said Robinson.

“By offering rents permanently capped to income and delivering unmatched security of tenure, it provides an unconditional safety net for society’s most vulnerable households.”.

In a recent development, office’s work has gained political attention. In November 2023, the Victorian Legislative Council debated the merits of the RRR approach, with the council’s Legal and Social Issues Committee urging the government to reconsider demolition and explore all refurbishment options.

The team can already claim a small victory. At Ascot Vale Estate, the first RRR case study released by Office, the development was quietly removed from the planned demolitions list on the Homes Victoria website and part of the estate has since been refurbished.

The estate is a collection of 57 three-storey brick housing blocks, built in 1947 and designed by renowned modernist architect and public housing advocate Best Overend during his time with the Housing Commission.

This gave Robinson and his team hope that the government would consider the alternatives if presented with the option.

“We have presented to Homes Victoria, we’ve presented to different ministers as well, and we’ve kind of heard that they are starting to look at retrofit some of their existing building stock,” said Robinson.

“It kind of suggests that perhaps they’re gonna prefer we show all of them. So we released the following studies on Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.”.

However, Barak Beacon Estate has since been demolished, and the construction of the redevelopment is due to complete by the end of the year.

Now the fate of Flemington Tower awaits a ruling from the High Court of Australia following a hearing last month.

A class action filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal on behalf of public housing residents in North Melbourne and Flemington is on its last appeal, after the Supreme Court of Victoria and Victorian Court of Appeal ruled in favour of demolition.

Meanwhile, the Liberal opposition has pledged to pause the HRRP if it wins office at the upcoming state election.

Robinson hopes he and his team have done enough, and continue to raise awareness about the issue.

“We’ve gotten to a point where we feel we can’t just keep putting out these reports,” he said.

In a recent development, “The papers we produced are quite dense and not for the general public. So what we’re now doing is translating that work into a series of publications, putting it in bookshops, and making it more accessible for the general public.”.

In a recent development, “We continue interviews with different residents, different advocates, different professionals, speaking with journalists and doing lectures. The idea is to bring awareness to what’s occurring, rather than us doing more reports.”.

He is also calling for a frank discussion in the architecture community about the redevelopment projects, which many of Australia’s prominent studios are working on.

“All the big-name architects are working on these estate renewals, some have even won awards as exemplar projects for these architects to promote their practice in terms of doing public good,” said Robinson.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s really hard to find anyone who’s willing to talk about why they’re doing it, or is it good, the displacement and environmental challenges. We’re alone.”.

Dezeen put Robinson’s claims to the Victorian state government, but was told it could not respond in the lead-up to the election.

When I first heard the HEDDphone D1 last November, I mentioned that the German audio tech giant had cracked the code. It's why they remain my top pick of the best-sounding wired, over-ear headphones at any price.

Sure, the HEDDphone D1 pack world-first driver technology and are hand-built in Germany, but for me that's not the main pull. It's the sound these things make! If you want neutral, balanced, slightly lean and mean but with exquisite detail, they're the best option at £599 – and a steal at £499!

That's because they offer the world’s first dynamic driver headphone with a Thin-Ply Carbon Diaphragm (TPCD). This is a genuinely special headphone, and a decent Black Friday price.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that the act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience.
  • For many, tattoos are much more than art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

Industry observers note that the act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Sources indicate that whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Industry observers note that psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

Sources indicate that there’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

It has been revealed that one 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

Recent findings suggest that however, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos revealed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It indicates, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a recent development, in a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings indicated that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.
