📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite the contemporary art world’s increased attention to women’s experiences and the politics of care in its public-facing programming, working mothers employed by London’s galleries and auction houses face widespread discrimination, according to a latest study. As reported by the Art Newspaper today, a survey of 50 employees working in the UK capital’s commercial art sector has found that, for many, having children comes at considerable professional cost.

The study, conducted by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi and published today in the European Journal of Cultural Studies, looked at the extent to which pregnancy and maternity affected career progression among art world workers. Moving beyond previous studies centered on fine artists or senior directors, it focused on lower-paid, non-artist roles such as sales, administration, and marketing. Related Articles Recent Key Departures at Phillips Point to a Pivot in Strategy The Year in Gallery Closures: A Collapse or a Transition to a Smarter Market?

In a recent development, roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s research, which also included 12 in-depth interviews, reveals an industry “marred by implicit and explicit expectations that often result in workers needing to choose between their careers and being parents,” they write. Three quarters of respondents felt that motherhood had impeded career advancement, while 20 percent remarked they had been explicitly denied promotion.

Sources indicate that the authors found poor and sometimes illegal practices across the industry, including employees being “managed” out of their roles while on maternity leave. Such practices, they note, are made possible by a lack of formal human resource structures—only half of the respondence worked for organizations with dedicated HR staff, and just 60 percent noted their workplace had a specific parental leave policy. They additionally blamed the art market’s pervasive culture of secrecy.

Class and wealth also play a role in shaping employee experience, the study suggests. For junior employees on modest salaries, the cost of childcare can make travel and attendance at evening events difficult and increase the likelihood of discrimination on the job. At the same time, a lack of resources makes challenging such discrimination daunting, with many women instead choosing to take a less senior position, move into freelance work, or leave the art world.

According to recent reports, roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s study spanned small galleries to multinational auction houses and found problems across the board. As they say in their report, “A lack of accountability pervades the sector.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins notes about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of major butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins indicates about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins states this concept can lend to beauty standards.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins claims you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Sources indicate that coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins states change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins notes, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

Carolina Zimbalist pours bioplastic over silk for Emma Watson's LACMA Gala dress

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (418 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artist Carolina Zimbalist has co-created a biomaterial dress with actress Emma Watson, who wore it at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s 15th annual Art+Film Gala.
  • Zimbalist, a graduate of the Parsons School of Design, employed a homemade bioplastic she frequently uses in her artistic works in order to create the one-of-a-kind garment, which comprises a longline bodice and floor-length skirt rendered in shades of red.
  • The petroleum-free poured-and-dried material, containing vegetable glycerin alongside naturally derived proteins such as pea powder, is layered over silk – a natural biopolymer itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Rich Stapleton.

Artist Carolina Zimbalist has co-created a biomaterial dress with actress Emma Watson, who wore it at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s 15th annual Art+Film Gala.

Zimbalist, a graduate of the Parsons School of Design, employed a homemade bioplastic she frequently uses in her artistic works in order to create the one-of-a-kind garment, which comprises a longline bodice and floor-length skirt rendered in shades of red.

The petroleum-free poured-and-dried material, containing vegetable glycerin alongside naturally derived proteins such as pea powder, is layered over silk – a natural biopolymer itself.

“The formulation draws on naturally derived proteins and other ingredients, with the exact composition varying depending on what I’m making,” Zimbalist told Dezeen.

“Very often I favour the usage of byproducts.”.

The material’s technical makeup lends itself to a distinctive aesthetic once poured and dried.

“My biomaterial creates sculptural forms and flexible surfaces that move with the body,” mentioned Zimbalist.

“The visual qualities are meant to draw greater interest in sustainable materials while remaining fundamentally artistic.”.

Zimbalist has variously referred to her recipe as a bioplastic, a biomaterial or a biopolymer, but now favours the latter to avoid negative associations with the term “plastic”.

“For years, I described my formulas as bioplastics, but about three seasons ago, I switched to ‘biomaterials’; when people hear ‘bioplastic’, they tend to focus on the plastic,” Zimbalist continued.

It has been revealed that “‘Biomaterial’ opens up a different conversation about what the material is and what it can become. All three terms apply, but they bring different associations – although biopolymer is the most technically accurate.”.

Zimbalist hopes that by experimenting with these natural materials, they can become a mainstream and accessible means of constructing garments beyond one-off pieces.

“The environmental benefits are something I’m developing along with the growing wave of biomaterial artists now assembling – I like to think we are presenting sustainable fashion in a way that inspires more interest beyond the fringes.”.

Zimbalist is no stranger to clothing celebrities: 2024 saw musician Chapelle Roan wear a hand-painted, garden-inspired dress that the artist made partially using seaweed.

As well as garments, the artist also creates ethereal and sculptural homeware, including lighting and vases.

Biomaterials are sweeping the fashion world, opening up opportunities for aesthetic and sustainable progress in a sector not historically known for its eco-friendliness.

Designers are increasingly finding ways to derive materials, fabrics and ornamentation from pioneering sources, including mycelium, tree cellulose and soil.

Tech Report: Judge Allows Lawsuit Over Allegedly Stolen Fra Angelico to Move Forward

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A New York judge has refused to throw out a lawsuit over a 15th-century Fra Angelico painting that the heirs to the Bic pen fortune say was stolen by their family chauffeur and later sold by the late art dealer Richard Feigen.
  • Sources indicate that in a decision dated October 26 and filed on November 16, Newly introduced York Supreme Court Justice James G.
  • “No family should lose a treasured work of art simply because the people who handled this stolen property were sophisticated dealmakers,” Luke Nikas, a lawyer for the Bich family, told ARTnews.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A New York judge has refused to throw out a lawsuit over a 15th-century Fra Angelico painting that the heirs to the Bic pen fortune say was stolen by their family chauffeur and later sold by the late art dealer Richard Feigen.

Sources indicate that in a decision dated October 26 and filed on November 16, Newly introduced York Supreme Court Justice James G. Clynes rejected an attempt by Feigen’s estate and associated businesses to get the case dismissed. Their main argument? The family had waited too long to sue.

“No family should lose a treasured work of art simply because the people who handled this stolen property were sophisticated dealmakers,” Luke Nikas, a lawyer for the Bich family, told ARTnews. The Bich family is determined to recover what belongs to them, and today’s decision is an important step toward achieving that result.” The ruling is good news for the Bich heirs, though there’s still a long way to go. The judge hasn’t decided who owns the painting, or even whether it was stolen. Related Articles Adam Lindemann Sued by Nature Conservancy for Allegedly Installing Julian Schnabel Sculpture Without Permission Fra Angelico's Restored Fiesole Altarpiece Returns to Its Original Church Home After Blockbuster Museum Show.

In a recent development, as ARTnews reported in April, the dispute centers on Saint Sixtus (ca. 1453–55), a painting by the Italian Renaissance master that Baron Marcel Bich, the founder of Bic, bought at Sotheby’s in 1972 for £130,000. The painting eventually passed to his son Bruno, who kept it in his Fifth Avenue apartment in Manhattan. Then, around 2006, it disappeared.

According to a lawsuit filed in March by Bruno’s three sons, Gonzalve, Charles, and Guillaume, the family’s chauffeur, Roy Morrow, stole the painting and sold it to Feigen for $3 million. The family says Morrow had no paperwork proving the painting was his, but Feigen bought it anyway and promptly insured it for $8.5 million, nearly three times what he’d paid.

Feigen, one of Newly introduced York’s best-known Old Master dealers before his death in 2021, later consigned the painting to Christie’s. In 2018, it was sold for $5.4 million to Chilean billionaire Álvaro Saieh and his wife, Ana Guzmán.

Sources indicate that the Bich brothers say they didn’t learn where the painting ended up until 2023. They asked for it back the following year, but Saieh and Guzmán refused. So the brothers sued, demanding the painting’s return, along with damages and money from its sale.

It has been revealed that feigen’s representatives tell a different story. In March, lawyers for his estate told Reuters that Morrow had signed a bill of sale saying he owned the painting. The Saiehs, meanwhile, have remarked they bought it in good faith, relying on Christie’s research.

Which brings us to the latest ruling.

Feigen’s lawyers argued that the family had simply waited too long to bring its claims. After all, Feigen bought the painting in 2006 and sold it in 2018. The brothers didn’t file their lawsuit until March 2026.

But stolen art can be a tricky business under Latest York law. Generally, when someone buys a stolen artwork in good faith, the clock doesn’t start ticking on a claim for its return until the rightful owner demands it back and the buyer refuses.

Things get more complicated when someone is accused of knowingly dealing in stolen property. The clock can start earlier, and Clynes noted there were too many unanswered questions about Feigen’s purchase to settle the matter now.

The judge also rejected, for now, an argument that the family had dragged its feet for so long that allowing the case to continue would be unfair. Lawyers call that laches. Both arguments can come up again later.

Feigen’s side did score one win. The judge dismissed claims against his revocable trust and its trustees because the family hadn’t shown enough to connect the trust to the money from the painting’s sale. The brothers can bring those claims again if they find more evidence.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This is proper packaging design, crafted as much for the fan experience as for protecting the controller.
  • The controller sits on a sliding shelf, so even getting it out is part of the experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I've never really been one for collectable controllers. I'm a fairly practical gamer, I suppose, and while I appreciate nice hardware design, I'm usually more interested in how a controller feels than how it looks, whether it has an on-brand D-pad or decals, for example. But opening the Tomb Raider 30th Anniversary Edition of 8BitDo's Ultimate 3 Controller has changed my mind a little, and I think it's largely down to the box.

This is proper packaging design, crafted as much for the fan experience as for protecting the controller. The Ultimate 3's box changes shape, opens, slides and reveals its secrets, almost like Lara Croft discovering some long-lost treasure, and I found myself enjoying the whole process far more than I expected. There's even a little golden envelope, almost hidden away, containing the instructions and a month of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate. It's all very Tomb Raider, and yes, I know I'm getting excited about a cardboard box.

The controller sits on a sliding shelf, so even getting it out is part of the experience. Then you start noticing the little design details. The faded brown-and-gold colourway features Lara silhouettes across it; there's a lovely golden metallic D-pad, and the whole thing looks like something recovered from an ancient tomb. The D-pad itself reminds me of a lost coin or compass face, which is a nice touch.

The metal D-pad disc did fall off once, but clipped back in fine. Do I expect that from a $120 controller? No, not really. Do I expect it from a $120 collectable controller where brand and design dominate? Yeah, probably.

In a recent development, I like that 8BitDo hasn't gone overboard with the branding; it feels like a well-made piece of gaming hardware, with the Tomb Raider design integrated rather than simply plastered on. The buttons are solid black, the sticks feel responsive, and the controller has a reassuring weight. The triggers have a nice solid feel, not too light but with a little flick as they snap back into place if released.

According to recent reports, then there's the stand, which I think is my favourite bit. The controller sits snugly in place, with a matching decal underneath, and it looks like you're slotting an ancient stone artefact into some sort of polar key and lock from the games. A soft orange LED glows when the controller charges, and suddenly I've got a little Tomb Raider shrine on my desk. I didn't think I needed one, but here we are.

What's clever about the design is that it gets at the look and feel of Tomb Raider without relying on Lara's face everywhere. The original games had such a distinctive visual identity: those angular environments, sandstone ruins, green foliage and Lara's turquoise costume, and it's a look that's stuck with me. The Ultimate 3 is more of a celebration of Lara across the series, but the colours, materials and little relic-like details bring back some of that atmosphere.

The less expensive Pro 3 Bluetooth Gamepad takes a more direct route back to the original game. Its design is inspired by the Lost Valley, with a jungle and ancient temple scene, and the charging stand picks up that weathered stone look. It's a different approach, and I rather like it. There's something about the Pro 3's shape, too, that reminds me of the old PS2 DualShock. It's lighter and a little more plasticky than the Ultimate 3, but still comfortable to hold, with a nice tactile feel to the buttons.

Industry observers note that this is the one I'd look at if I were playing on Switch 2, especially if you want to revisit the Tomb Raider: Definitive Survivor Trilogy on Nintendo's console. It's a good-looking pad; the Lost Valley artwork is lovely, and the included stand gives it personality when you're not playing. It's also a capable modern controller, with TMR sticks and Hall-effect triggers, so you don't feel like you're buying it purely for the artwork.

It has been revealed that but I keep glancing back at the Ultimate 3. The Pro 3 is perfectly good and arguably has a stronger connection to the original 1996 game, but it doesn't quite have the same sense of occasion. Its unboxing is much more straightforward, and I never thought I'd say this, but I'd happily pay the extra for the Ultimate 3 packaging. The fact that the controller feels better made is a bonus.

Sources indicate that I've always thought of collectable gaming hardware as something that looks nice in a display cabinet but doesn't necessarily earn its place in everyday use, and I think that's what has surprised me most about these two pads. The Ultimate 3 has made me reconsider my somewhat cynical approach to collectable controllers, as it’s a gamepad I actually want to use, but I also like having it on my desk, and the whole thing was designed with that in mind.

According to recent reports, switch 2 players shouldn't feel left out. The Pro 3 is a lovely alternative, and if you're particularly fond of the original Tomb Raider, there's a lot to like about its Lost Valley design. But if you're after the full treasure-hunter experience, the Ultimate 3 is the one that has me reaching for my wallet. And that's something I really didn't expect to say about a controller.

The new Grand Theft Auto arrived this week, the messianic reward after 13 long years, offering the best-rendered version of the series’ standing promise: anything, within the scope of its metropolis and the player’s imagination. I watched my cousin paint a house for his avatar’s girlfriend, then hop in a car and drive to the Bass Museum. Or rather, to the Vice City Museum of Art, the faithful replica of it in Vice City, the game’s fictional Miami.

According to recent reports, rockstar teased that Grand Theft Auto VI would boast the franchise’s sharpest graphics yet, and the claim was not exaggerated. The Vice Museum of Art captures the Bass’s signature civic Art Deco style: a pale limestone facade (the real stuff was quarried in the Florida Keys) and, as far as I could tell, even the carved decorative relief around the entry. It’s a far cry from the series’ earliest entries, when a building like this would have been a smooth beige box; here, the facade looks textured. We parked and admired its public art: a riff on Miami Mountain, a tower of boulders by Ugo Rondinone permanently installed in Collins Park, outside the Bass. Part of Rondinone’s “Mountain” series, it’s made of garishly clashing fluorescent rocks stacked high and probably visible from space. The Vice City version has swapped stone for emojis: winking, crying, smiling. Related Articles Judge Allows Lawsuit Over Allegedly Stolen Fra Angelico to Move Forward How do Artworks Acquire Value? Latest York Art Dealers David Nolan and Anton Svyatsky Weigh In.

Vice City may be hiding another Easter egg for art heads. Months ago, a screenshot circulated online from an expansion for Grand Theft Auto Online, showing a fresh character in a shirt with an “Art Oregano” logo. It’s a safe bet that it’s a nod to Art Basel Miami Beach, held at the Miami Beach Convention Center, since it’s set in the same font as the fair’s. The herby homage was well received. “I hope he’ll be in GTA 6 having his own little art studio or something,” wrote one Reddit user. Another added, “I can’t wait to wear this shirt to Art Basel this year, if I can pull myself away from GTA6.”.

Art Basel Miami Beach runs December 4-6; keep an eye out for Art Oregano shirts. And, perhaps, as players make it further into the notoriously long game, a new version of Art Oregano may appear.

In a recent development, I couldn’t personally verify whether the game includes a replica of the fair, with NPCs entering and exiting, as the Vice Museum did. We’d spent the momentous night mundanely, mostly comparing paint swatches. All of it in line with what viral clips suggest: the game’s characters can do drugs and rob banks—chaos, generally speaking—but we’d rather have time to drive with no destination in mind.

Before I left, my cousin regretfully canceled our plans to visit the Guggenheim on Saturday. He has to work.

Yuri Suzuki 3D-prints miniature rollercoaster and Ferris wheel for kinetic Onomatopia exhibition

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Chris Kidall Park (unless otherwise stated).
  • Designer Yuri Suzuki drew on his childhood fascination with amusement parks for the Onomatopia exhibition, which features playful dioramas with their own soundtracks and indicates how theme parks “bring together architecture, sound, movement and human experience”.
  • On show at the Osh Gallery in London’s Angel neighbourhood, the exhibition features five models, a short film and reference materials from Suzuki’s own archive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Chris Kidall Park (unless otherwise stated).

Designer Yuri Suzuki drew on his childhood fascination with amusement parks for the Onomatopia exhibition, which features playful dioramas with their own soundtracks and indicates how theme parks “bring together architecture, sound, movement and human experience”.

On show at the Osh Gallery in London’s Angel neighbourhood, the exhibition features five models, a short film and reference materials from Suzuki’s own archive.

The dioramas – a Ferris wheel, rollercoaster, helter-skelter, dodgems and carousel – resemble some of Suzuki‘s earlier work, such as the interactive Sonic Bloom installation in London.

“The ideas have existed in my sketchbooks for the last couple of years and have gradually developed through a series of my public art projects,” Suzuki told Dezeen.

“I’ve always been interested in expanding the scale of my sound sculptures, imagining how they might eventually become architectural structures or even full-scale amusement park rides.”.

The designer 3D-printed the kinetic sculptures, which move and are accompanied by their own soundtracks, from polylactic acid (PLA) plastic.

“The dioramas are mainly made using 3D-printed materials, alongside modified HO-scale miniature structures,” he noted.

“I had picked up traditional amusement park components – roller coaster, ferris wheel, helter-skelter, carousel, and dodge cars – to visualise my ideas for sound sculptures and architectural structures that could potentially be realised on a larger scale in the future.”.

Suzuki has been drawn to amusement parks all his life, and with Onomatopia he wanted to explore how they could help create a utopian city.

“I’ve been fascinated by theme parks since I was a child, particularly Disneyland, but also the relationship between amusement parks, world expos and urban planning, from Coney Island as explored in Rem Koolhaas’s Delirious Latest York to the 1889 Paris Exposition,” he explained.

“I had the opportunity to work with Disney Imagineering, who create Disney parks, and I became particularly interested in Walt Disney’s original vision for EPCOT (Experimental Prototype of Community of Tomorrow),” Suzuki continued.

“It imagined an ideal city rather than simply a theme park, and Onomatopia is my own attempt to imagine a utopian city shaped by sound, drawing on my experience creating public installations.”.

Suzuki, who is known for his sound design, has previously created pieces such as an acoustic playground in Shanghai and a “trumpet-like” San Francisco art installation.

“For me, theme parks and expos are fascinating because they bring together architecture, sound, movement and human experience within an imagined world, almost like an experiment in creating a utopian city,” Suzuki explained.

The designer drew on his experience of working on a large-scale sound design when creating these smaller versions of his sculptures.

“Over the last couple of years I have been involved in some large city development projects, such as creating Metropolis Symphony for One Bangkok and my initial involvement in planning around the V&A East (East Bank) development,” Suzuki mentioned.

“I’ve become increasingly interested in how sound can shape public spaces, and my own idea of utopia is a place where sound contributes to wellbeing and encourages communication between people, beyond the boundaries of language and culture.”.

Onomatopia is on show at Osh Gallery, The Old Sorting House, 46 Essex Road, London from 10 November 2026 to 7 January 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sources indicate that sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Sources indicate that going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

It has been revealed that stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

In a recent development, light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Industry observers note that light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Sources indicate that diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

El Greco Masterpiece Gets Its Colors Back After More Than 400 Years

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • King Philip II of Spain wasn’t particularly impressed with El Greco‘s The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion when he first saw it.
  • It has been revealed that A painstaking nine-month restoration, recently finished, has found the monumental painting looking considerably more like the one El Greco envisioned.
  • According to recent reports, the restoration was conducted at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery, under the supervision of Rafael Alonso, an 81-year-old former Prado Museum restorer, who has spent decades working on El Greco’s paintings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

King Philip II of Spain wasn’t particularly impressed with El Greco‘s The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion when he first saw it. The following four centuries of dirt, varnish, and enthusiastic repainting hadn’t done the picture any favors, either.

It has been revealed that A painstaking nine-month restoration, recently finished, has found the monumental painting looking considerably more like the one El Greco envisioned. The muddy browns and sickly greens that had dulled the picture for generations are gone. In their place are brilliant blues, reds, yellows, and purples, along with a newfound depth that had been buried beneath grime. Related Articles AI Model Reveals Upcoming Information About Authorship of 17th-Century El Greco Altarpiece 15th-Century Bellini Altarpiece in Venice to Be Restored While the Public Watches.

According to recent reports, the restoration was conducted at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery, under the supervision of Rafael Alonso, an 81-year-old former Prado Museum restorer, who has spent decades working on El Greco’s paintings. The project was supported by the Fundacion Callia in partnership with Spain’s Patrimonio Nacional, which oversees the country’s royal collections.

The results were reported in detail by El País, whose writer followed the restoration from the painting’s removal from El Escorial in February through its finished restoration in October. And what a job it was.

Alonso had initially expected the restoration to take about four months. But once he and fellow restorer Adela Murgui began cleaning the enormous canvas, which measures nearly 15 feet high and 10 feet wide, they discovered that its condition was far worse than even feared.

Industry observers note that “When I put the cotton to the painting, my heart sank,” Alonso told El País. Centuries of varnish and repainting had darkened the colors and flattened the composition. In the 19th century, he explained, painters had simply painted over damaged areas, often adding their own interpretations of what El Greco intended.

The restorers spent months carefully stripping away those additions, revealing the original paint beneath. Afterward, the repaired the damaged areas using soluble materials, taking pains not to add anything that couldn’t be removed later.

The restoration is particularly striking given the painting’s rather unhappy beginnings.

In a recent development, el Greco painted The Martyrdom between 1580 and 1582 for the basilica at El Escorial, Philip II’s vast monastery and palace outside Madrid. The king wanted a powerful statement of Catholic faith, while the artist hoped the commission might secure him a permanent position as a court painter.

Neither’s wish was totally granted.

Sources indicate that rather than concentrate on the grisly execution of Saint Maurice and his fellow Christian soldiers, El Greco pushed the violence into the background. Up front, he placed a group of handsome soldiers in brightly colored clothing, their elongated bodies and theatrical poses exemplary of the skills he had learned in Venice and Rome.

Philip II apparently admired the painting’s quality, paying the artist a substantial sum of 800 ducats, but felt it wasn’t right for its intended religious setting. The work was relegated to another room, and El Greco never clinched the royal appointment he’d hoped for.

The painting stayed there for most of the next 444 years, apart from a trip to Madrid for an exhibition in 1999, all the while gradually losing most of its remarkable color and atmosphere.

The restoration also marks another achievement for the Fundacion Callia, founded by Carmen Reviriego, which has helped restore works by Zurbarán, Rubens, Brueghel the Elder, Velázquez, and others through its partnership with Madrid’s Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando. According to El País, the foundation has helped mobilize €5 million for the preservation of artworks.

When ARTnews spoke with Reviriego in March, she described Callia as an “incubator of patrons,” bringing together collectors and philanthropists from Spain, Latin America, and beyond. Her goal is to encourage a stronger culture of private support for the arts in a country that has traditionally relied heavily on public funding.

Industry observers note that reviriego had specifically mentioned The Martyrdom during that interview as an example of the work the foundation hoped to support. “El Greco was the Jeff Koons or Damien Hirst of his day,” she told ARTnews this week, “and Phillip II was the most power man and greatest patron of the 16th century.”.

According to recent reports, there’s a nice historical symmetry here. Reviriego argued that great works of art are rarely the achievement of an artist alone. Without patrons, many wouldn’t exist at all. She pointed to the Royal Collections themselves, built in part through the patronage of Philip II, the very king who commissioned The Martyrdom more than four centuries ago. Now, private patronage has helped give that painting a new life.

It has been revealed that for Alonso, meanwhile, the completed restoration marks something of a farewell. After decades spent working on El Greco’s paintings, he told El País that The Martyrdom was the last of the artist’s great masterpieces still awaiting restoration.

The newly restored painting is expected to go on temporary display at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery before returning to El Escorial. This time, visitors will get a much better idea of what Philip II saw more than four centuries ago.

#80376. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

📅 09 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance.
  • Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells.
  • Recent findings suggest that although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Recent findings suggest that although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

In a recent development, now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a massive-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Sources indicate that does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Industry observers note that beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

It has been revealed that thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American fast-food chain Chipotle has launched a hoodie with a hidden, insulated pocket built for one highly specific purpose.

The novelty streetwear garment was designed to keep burritos both warm and concealed while sneaking them into the cinema for illicit mid-movie snacking.

Accessed via a subtle zip at the top of the hoodie’s front pouch, the pocket can also squeeze in an entire burrito bowl or a set of tacos, Chipotle claims, although the logistics of that might be trickier.

Kirby Ann Connell, the firm’s senior director of social and influencers, said the launch was inspired by real stories of people smuggling elaborate Chipotle meals into the cinema.

Sources indicate that “Movie nights deserve real, craveable food,” she said. “And since our fans were already sneaking Chipotle to theatres, we figured we’d make it a little easier.”.

“Sometimes innovation is as simple as putting a burrito pocket in a hoodie,” she added.

The limited-edition Sneak It In hoodie features an oversized fit to conceal any bulky contraband, plus a dedicated napkin pocket for any spills.

It comes in three colourways: Nothing To See Here Black, No Burrito Here Brown and Got the Goods Gray.

Chipotle is the latest brand to create novelty streetwear as a marketing stunt.

Other offerings include KFC’s Pickle Puffer, Lego-shaped Crocs and Aldi’s Potato Jacket.

#80374. The 16 Most Expensive Artworks Ever Sold at Auction

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4228 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Artnews ↗ Open Full Page

The 16 Most Expensive Artworks Ever Sold at Auction

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4228 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that auction records make for great headlines, like the 2026 banner sale of Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which topped $236.4 million at Sotheby’s.
  • Look at the list of the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, and you’ll see more than just a parade of billionaires with good taste (or at least expensive taste).
  • Recent findings suggest that yes, Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million, but is it really a Leonardo?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that auction records make for great headlines, like the 2026 banner sale of Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which topped $236.4 million at Sotheby’s. There’s a thrill in watching numbers climb into the stratosphere, each sale another reminder that, in the art market, money has a way of bending reality. But the price of a painting has never been the most interesting thing about it.

Look at the list of the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, and you’ll see more than just a parade of billionaires with good taste (or at least expensive taste). You’ll see a history of ideas—what mattered to the artists who made them, what obsessed the collectors who chased them, and how we decide, decades or centuries later, which works still hold power.

Recent findings suggest that yes, Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million, but is it really a Leonardo? Picasso’s Women of Algiers, Pollock’s Number 7A, 1948, and Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn all shattered records, with the Pollock work shooting far beyond its $100 million estimate when it came to auction at Christie’s in May 2026 in a sale of works from the S. I. Newhouse collection. But these works’ real value has nothing to do with what someone was willing to pay on a given evening at Christie’s. The best art—the kind that shifts culture, lingers in your mind, and changes how you see the world—exists in a space money can’t touch.

But of course, once a work crosses a threshold, there’s something almost inevitable about the price spiral. With each record-breaking sale, the bar gets set higher, the stakes get sharper, and the frenzy deepens. The game has changed, but in a way, the auction houses are just as much a stage for the spectacle as for the art itself. Every price tag opens the door to another possibility. If one work can sell for $450 million, what’s to stop the next from reaching half a billion—or more? With so many players in the game, all vying for the ultimate cultural trophy, the numbers have a way of multiplying faster than the logic behind them.

Recent findings suggest that and yet, the more those numbers rise, the further they drift from the essential thing that makes art so valuable: the art itself. High prices can make us think we’re in the presence of something transcendent, but it’s the work that holds the power, not the price. So, here’s the list. The numbers are staggering, but don’t get too caught up in them. The real story is in the art itself.

According to recent reports, A version of this article was first published on November 19, 2025. It was last updated on November 20, 2026.

Sold for $119.9 million at Sotheby’s Upcoming York in May 2012.

When it sold for $107 million at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York, Munch’s pastel The Scream (1895), one of the four versions—two painted and two in pastel—that he made of the same subject, became the most expensive work ever to be sold at a public auction, stealing the trophy from Picasso’s 1932 Nude, Green Leaves and Bust, which sold at Christie’s in 2010 for $106.5 million.

At the time, it was the only version of The Scream still in private hands; its seller was Petter Olsen, a Norwegian businessman whose father, Thomas, was Munch’s friend and patron. The picture, which opened at $40 million, sparked a 12-minute bidding war, with wide-eyed potential buyers both in the salesroom and on the phones. According to the Wall Street Journal, its buyer was investor Leon Black, a trustee at the Museum of Modern Art, where The Scream later went on view.

According to recent reports, after the sale Olsen, described by Art in America as “the wild-haired and bespectacled seller,” read a statement that tied the work to climate change and global warming: “The Scream for me demonstrates the horrifying moment when man realizes his impact on nature and the irreversible changes that he has initiated, making the planet increasingly uninhabitable. . . . More death, less life. And very few lifeboats left as we go down.”.

Sold for $121 million at Christie’s Latest York in November 2024.

In a recent development, the “crown jewel” of the auction market in 2024 (as Christie’s so humbly put it) was perhaps the finest example of a subject that Magritte revisited more than 25 times throughout his career: an otherworldly scene showing a house on tree-lined street at night. But instead being enveloped in darkness, the sky above the trees is impossibly blue, with significant, cottony clouds floating by. This 1954 version of Empire of Light, which sold for $121 million and came from the collection of designer and philanthropist Mica Ertegun, set a latest record for Magritte’s work at auction.

After the sale, Christie’s chairman of 20th and 21st century art Alex Rotter mentioned the house that evening had adopted a “masterpiece approach” to this sale. “In a market that is not so easy to maneuver, we thought that if we present the greatest works we can get … these are the best examples,” Rotter said, admitting that the auction had its share of lots that didn’t catch collectors’ attention. But “the works that we put all the emphasis behind really proved us right. They had multiple bidders and showed that a market based on individual taste is on the rise.”.

Sold for $137.7 million at Christie’s Fresh York in November 2022.

According to recent reports, cézanne’s deliciously rich landscape of the French countryside and his beloved Mont Sainte-Victoire is the second of five works from the Paul Allen sale at Christie’s to make this list. When the hammer fell, Mont Sainte-Victoire (1888–90) doubled Cézanne’s previous auction high of $60.5 million, for a still life from the collection of John Hay Whitney.

Like Cézanne’s best works, Mont Sainte-Victoire breaks aspects of the world—in this case, a French mountain—into shapes shaded with color, as though they were three-dimensional geometrical forms. In that way, Cézanne paved the way for Cubist artists such as Pablo Picasso and George Braque, who would push his innovations even further toward abstraction.

Sold for $139.3 million at Sotheby’s New York in November 2023.

Recent findings suggest that woman with a Watch (1932), one of Picasso’s many paintings of his mistress Marie-Thérèse Walter, became the second most expensive work by the artist ever sold at auction when it fetched $139 million at Sotheby’s in 2023. The canvas, from the collection of late philanthropist Emily Fisher Landau, drew intense bidding before selling to a phone bidder represented by Sotheby’s head of global fine art, Brooke Lampley.

Woman with a Watch had a rarefied provenance, changing hands just a few times since Picasso painted it in 1932. It was acquired by Landau in 1968 from Pace Gallery, which had purchased it from Switzerland’s Galerie Beyeler two years earlier.

Industry observers note that pictures of Walter typically go for top dollar. In 2010, Nude, Green Leaves and Bust—also painted in 1932—broke records at $106.5 million. Still, the most expensive Picasso of all time is a work that does not depict Walter. But more on that in a bit.

Sold for $140.8 million at Poly International Auction Co., Ltd., Beijing in December 2017.

Qi Baishi’s Twelve Screens of Landscapes (1925) shattered records in 2017, selling for RMB 931.5 million ($140.8 million) at Beijing Poly Auction and making it the most expensive Chinese artwork ever sold at auction. The bidding war lasted over 20 minutes, with more than 60 bid increments before a Chinese collector secured the 12-panel piece.

Each 70-inch panel captures a sweeping vista from Qi’s travels across China. Originally displayed at his solo exhibition in 1954 and later featured in a memorial show in 1958, the set of panels was kept by Qi’s pupil, Xiuyi Guo, before resurfacing at auction.

It has been revealed that A similar version of Twelve Screens of Landscapes, painted around 1932 as a gift to Kuomintang general Wang Zuanxu, resides in the Chongqing Museum. The set sold in 2017 was the only one in private hands at the time, making it a rarity.

Sold for $141.3 million at Christie’s Fresh York in May 2015.

Alberto Giacometti’s Pointing Man (1947) became the most expensive sculpture ever sold at auction when it fetched $141.3 million at Christie’s New York in May 2015. The life-size bronze, standing at more than five and a half feet tall, was sold by real estate magnate Sheldon Solow, surpassing Giacometti’s previous auction record of $104.3 million, which was set at Sotheby’s London five years earlier by Walking Man I (1960).

One of six casts made by the artist (not counting an additional artist’s proof), this particular Pointing Man had been held privately for 45 years before the sale. Four of those casts reside in major museums, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Tate in London, which made this auction a prime opportunity for collectors. Similar sculptures by Giacometti depicting skeletal, elongated figures have likewise sold for major sums.

At the time, Christie’s head Pylkkänen called the piece “one of the finest works of art I have had the honor to handle.” Whoever bought the piece clearly agreed about its quality.

Sold for $142.4 million at Christie’s New York in November 2013.

Francis Bacon’s Three Studies of Lucian Freud (1969) briefly became the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction when it sold for $142.4 million at Christie’s Upcoming York in November 2013. The triptych surpassed the previous record, held by Edvard Munch’s pastel The Scream, which sold for $119.9 million at Sotheby’s in 2012 (and which also appears on this list, above).

Bacon’s three-panel portrait—each part stands six and a half feet tall—depicts Bacon’s longtime friend and artistic rival, Lucian Freud, in a series of contorted poses. The piece had an unusual history: its panels were separated by a dealer in the 1970s and remained apart for 15 years before being reunited by a collector in 1989.

Industry observers note that the work was expected to sell for over $85 million, but after a five-minute bidding war, it was secured by New York’s Acquavella Galleries. In a strategic move, Christie’s shifted the Bacon painting to the ninth lot of the evening to allow unsuccessful bidders a chance at other works—an approach that proved successful, contributing to the auction house’s record-breaking $691.6 million total for the night.

Shortly after the sale, the anonymous buyer lent the triptych to the Portland Art Museum for public viewing from December 2013 to March 2014.

Sold for $149 million at Christie’s New York in November 2022.

Sources indicate that in November 2022, an early 20th-century masterpiece by Georges Seurat, Models (Small Version) (1888), sold for a staggering $149 million at Christie’s Latest York. The painting, depicting three nude figures in Seurat’s signature pointillist style, was one of the rarest privately-owned works by the artist. It came from the collection of Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen and was expected to surpass $100 million at auction.

The bidding opened at $75 million, drawing competition from four bidders, including specialists representing clients in Latest York and Asia. After several minutes of heated back-and-forth, the work hammered at $130 million, with Christie’s Asia chairman securing the piece for a final total of $149 million, including fees. The sale set a new auction record for Seurat, shattering his previous high of $34 million, achieved in 2018 for The Harbor at Grandcamp(1885).

Sources indicate that the last time Models (Small Version) appeared on the market was in 1970, when it fetched just over $1 million at Christie’s. Prior to Allen’s ownership, it had belonged to the influential collector John Quinn, a champion of modernist artists in the early 20th century.

Sold for $157.2 million at Sotheby’s New York in May 2018.

Amedeo Modigliani’s Reclining Nude (on Her Left Side) (1917), one of the artist’s most celebrated nudes, sold for $157.2 million at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York in 2018. The total price, including the buyer’s premium, followed a hammer bid of $139 million, which fell just short of its undisclosed estimate of $150 million. Despite this, the sale set a record for the most expensive artwork ever sold at Sotheby’s at the time.

Sources indicate that the large-scale canvas—depicting a nude woman gazing over her shoulder at the viewer—was the star lot of the auction house’s Impressionist and Modern art sale. Bidding opened at $125 million with auctioneer Helena Newman presiding over the room. The winning bid came from a client on the phone with Simon Shaw, Sotheby’s co-head of Impressionist and Modern art worldwide, after a subdued and measured exchange.

According to recent reports, the work belongs to Modigliani’s groundbreaking series of reclining nudes, painted between 1916 and 1919. When first exhibited in 1917 at Parisian dealer Berthe Weill’s gallery, these erotic paintings caused such a scandal that police shut down the show after just two days. At the time, only two drawings were sold.

While the sale price was extraordinary, it did not surpass Modigliani’s auction record, which remains with Reclining Nude (1917–18), sold at Christie’s in 2015 for $170.4 million to Chinese collector Liu Yiqian. Sotheby’s, however, positioned Reclining Nude (on Her Left Side) as a transformative work, with Simon Shaw stating, “There is the nude before Modigliani, and there is the nude after Modigliani.”.

Sold for $170.4 million at Christie’s Latest York in November 2015.

Amedeo Modigliani’s Reclining Nude (1917–18) shattered expectations at Christie’s New York in 2015, selling for $170.4 million, more than doubling the artist’s previous auction record of $70.7 million. The work, which carried an on-request estimate of over $100 million, became the second-most expensive painting ever sold at auction at the time.

It has been revealed that the sale took place during Christie’s curated evening auction, “The Artist’s Muse,” which aimed to build buzz around 20th-century masterpieces. Despite a mixed night—with several major lots, including works by Willem de Kooning and Lucian Freud, failing to sell—the Modigliani nude electrified the room. Bidding was fierce, ultimately concluding with a Chinese collector securing the work via telephone, as revealed by Pylkkänen after the sale. (The collector was later revealed to be Chinese billionaire businessman Liu Yiqian.).

It has been revealed that reclining Nude is part of Modigliani’s celebrated series of reclining nudes, painted between 1916 and 1919. These works, revolutionary in their sensuality and bold in their approach to form, scandalized Paris when first exhibited at Berthe Weill’s gallery in 1917, leading to the show’s abrupt closure by police. Today, they are considered among the most important contributions to the modern nude tradition.

Sources indicate that the sale of Reclining Nude was a high point in an otherwise uneven auction, which totaled $491.4 million—above its $440 million low estimate but falling far short of the $705.8 million brought in by a similar sale earlier that year. While other records were set that night—including for works by Gustave Courbet, Balthus, and Roy Lichtenstein—the Modigliani painting stood out as the undeniable star of the evening, solidifying the artist’s status as one of the most sought-after names in the art market.

Sold for $179.4 million at Christie’s Fresh York in May 2015.

Industry observers note that pablo Picasso’s Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’) (1955) set a latest auction record in 2015 when it sold for $179.4 million at Christie’s New York, becoming the most expensive painting ever sold at auction at the time. The painting, the final and most intricate piece in Picasso’s 15-work “Women of Algiers” series (1954–55), had an on-request estimate of around $140 million but soared past that figure after deep bidding.

Recent findings suggest that the competition for the masterpiece played out entirely over the phone, with then-Christie’s executives Loic Gouzer and Brett Gorvy representing rival bidders. Pylkkänen, serving as auctioneer, declared “Still many people in the game” as bidding climbed past $140 million. Eventually, Gorvy’s bidder emerged victorious with a hammer price of $160 million, drawing cheers from the audience.

The “Women of Algiers” series was inspired by Eugène Delacroix’s 1834 masterpiece of the same name. Created in response to the Nationalist uprising in Algeria against French colonial rule, the series reflects Picasso’s fascination with both European Orientalist art and the evolving political landscape of the time. The version here is considered the most elaborate and fully realized of the set.

Recent findings suggest that the painting had a notable provenance, originally acquired by New York collectors Victor and Sally Ganz directly from legendary dealer Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler in 1956. It first appeared at auction in 1997, when it sold for $31.9 million—meaning its value increased nearly sixfold in less than two decades.

According to recent reports, while Christie’s maintained confidentiality regarding the winning bidder, reports later suggested that the buyer was former Qatari Prime Minister Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani. The sale reinforced Picasso’s dominance in the art market, cementing Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’) as one of the defining auction moments of the decade.

Sold for $181.2 million at Christie’s New York in May 2026.

Sources indicate that this 11-foot-wide painting by Jackson Pollock came to auction at Christie’s with both a first-class provenance and remarkable historical cachet. Pollock painted the work in 1948, the year after he first devised his drip painting technique, in which the artist flung his paint at the canvas rather than applying it directly using his brush. The technique distanced Pollock’s hand from his painting, leaving the application of his paint to chance.

Before he owned Sotheby’s, businessman A. Alfred Taubman owned the painting, selling it to publishing magnate S. I. Newhouse in 2000. In 2026, nearly a decade after Newhouse’s death, the painting headed to sale at Christie’s with a $100 million estimate, poising it to break Pollock’s record. At the time of the Christie’s auction, the painting hadn’t been seen publicly since 1977.

In a recent development, the work ended up shooting far beyond its estimate and becoming one of the most expensive paintings ever sold. Bidding opened at $80 million, and following 60 bids, the painting hammered at $157 million. With fees, the total rose to $181.2 million.

On November 18, 2026, Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), a picture of sunlit trees set against oncoming storm clouds, sold for $190.4 million (including fees) at Sotheby’s. The cover lot for the auction house’s Blaquier-Arrieta collection sale, which the house had billed as “legendary,” it set a new auction record for the Dutch painter. The reported buyer was dealer William Acquavella.

Recent findings suggest that the artist’s previous record of $117.2 million was set at Christie’s in November 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888), a landscape from the collection of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen, sold for $102 million. The new result beat that by $73.2 million, a jump of 62.4 percent in just four years.

It has been revealed that that the sale happened at all was a victory for Sotheby’s. Just days before the auction, descendants of Samuel Fischer, the German Jewish publisher who once owned the painting, challenged its sale, arguing that their family had been forced to part with it in Amsterdam in 1936 because of Nazi persecution. Sotheby’s disputed the claim, pointing to archival records showing the painting had sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, around $22,000 at the time, which it considered a fair market price. After several days of talks, the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the Fischer heirs reached an agreement, clearing the painting’s title.

Painted shortly after Van Gogh arrived at Auvers-sur-Oise in May 1890, Blossoming Chestnut Trees is among the 70-plus paintings (and more than 50 drawings) that the artist made there before taking his own life only two months later. It was also one of only eight Auvers landscapes still in private hands, according to research cited by the Art Newspaper.

Industry observers note that the electric scene, with its thick brushwork, also hadn’t been seen in decades. It was last exhibited at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in 1964 before Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro and Nelly Arrieta Blaquier, bought it in 1975—the kind of provenance and scarcity that fuels record-breaking prices like this one.—Daniel Cassady.

Sold for $195 million at Christie’s New York in May 2022.

Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn, one of the most iconic images in modern art, became the most expensive 20th-century artwork ever sold at auction when it fetched $195 million at Christie’s Upcoming York in 2022. The silkscreen portrait, based on a publicity still of Marilyn Monroe from the 1953 film Niagara, is part of Warhol’s famous “Shot Marilyn” series—named after a 1964 incident when performance artist Dorothy Podber fired a gun at a stack of Warhol’s canvases.

The work was the star lot of the evening, drawing competition from four bidders, including three on the phone and one in the room. Art dealer Larry Gagosian, bidding in person, ultimately secured the painting with a hammer price of $170 million, well below its $200 million estimate.

The “Shot Marilyn” works are among Warhol’s most coveted pieces, with only five versions in existence. This particular portrait had been in a private collection for five decades, coming from the estate of Swiss dealers Thomas and Doris Ammann. With no financial guarantee, its sale marked a major moment for both the Warhol market and the broader contemporary art market.

In surpassing the $179.4 million record set by Picasso’s Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’) (1955) in 2015, Shot Sage Blue Marilyn reaffirmed Warhol’s place at the pinnacle of modern art valuations. While some experts saw the sale as a watershed moment, others noted that privately brokered transactions for blue-chip artworks have long exceeded the $200 million mark.

Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16) became the second-most expensive artwork ever sold at auction when it achieved $236.4 million at Sotheby’s in November 2025, surpassing Klimt’s previous records and setting a latest high for any work of modern art. The full-length portrait, one of only two named Klimt commissions in private hands, was the undisputed centerpiece of the sale of the Leonard A. Lauder Collection.

Bidding opened at $130 million and unfolded over 20 tense minutes, narrowing to two phone bidders represented by Sotheby’s specialists David Galperin and Julian Dawes. Dawes’s bidder ultimately won with a hammer price of $205 million, prompting applause in the salesroom and marking the most expensive lot ever handled by Sotheby’s. The result vaulted past Picasso’s Les Femmes d’Alger (Version ‘O’), which had held the record for a modern artwork at $179.4 million since 2015. Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn, meanwhile, made global headlines when it skirted the $200 million mark in 2022.

Industry observers note that the painting was commissioned by one of Klimt’s most key patron families, survived wartime confiscation, and was restituted in 1948 before entering Lauder’s collection in the 1980s. Estimated in excess of $150 million, it had been widely expected to challenge the artist’s previous high. Instead, it rewrote the record books—cementing Klimt as one of the few early-modern painters consistently capable of commanding nine-figure prices in today’s market, and potentially opening the door for even more masterpieces to break the $200 million barrier.

Sold for $450.3 million at Christie’s Newly introduced York in November 2017.

In a landmark moment in the art world, Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi (c. 1500) set a upcoming record for the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction, fetching an astonishing $450.3 million at Christie’s in New York in November 2017. The sale, which took place in a packed salesroom at Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, was driven by an intense 19-minute bidding war.

Bidding began in earnest at $100 million—which was also the guarantee—and escalated rapidly from there, with cheers and applause breaking out as the painting crossed the $200 million threshold. Pylkkanen, again serving as auctioneer, skillfully kept the crowd engaged as bids climbed incrementally in the final moments. At one point, the bidding reached $350 million, before finally settling at $400 million, with an additional $50 million in fees for the buyer.

According to recent reports, the Salvator Mundi’s journey to the auction block was filled with intrigue, including debates over its authenticity and a controversial restoration by conservator Dianne Modestini. Despite these uncertainties, the painting’s remarkable backstory and its connection to Leonardo da Vinci—whether authentic or not—captivated buyers. The work had once sold for just $1,175 in 2005, when it was attributed to a follower of Leonardo, but was later restored and re-attributed to the master himself.

Recent findings suggest that the sale marked a culmination of a carefully orchestrated marketing campaign by Christie’s, which included a global tour and celebrity endorsements, such as Patti Smith and Leonardo DiCaprio. The Salvator Mundi’s upcoming auction price far eclipsed the previous record-holder, Pablo Picasso’s Women of Algiers (Version O) (1955), which had sold for $179 million earlier that year.

This sale marked not only a record-breaking moment for the auction house but also highlighted the increasingly influential role of market value in the art world, where the price tag may overshadow the painting’s historical and artistic significance.

The buyer of Salvator Mundi was revealed a month after to the sale to be Saudi Arabian crown prince Mohammed Bin Salman, with quiet prepares for it to eventually go on view in Riyadh.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

According to recent reports, wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:.

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner looks suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

Industry observers note that if imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Industry observers note that feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

In a recent development, shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

Sources indicate that no respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

It has been revealed that if they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

According to recent reports, if your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

Recent findings suggest that true love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

In a recent development, still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

It has been revealed that are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.
